chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 1 — Venice. A street
paragraphs: [Enter Roderigo and Iago.]
RODERIGO. Enough — don't tell me that. I take it very badly that you, Iago, who've had the run of my purse as if its strings were yours to open, knew about this.
IAGO. God's blood, you won't listen to me! If I ever even dreamed of such a thing, you can loathe me.
RODERIGO. You told me you hated him.

IAGO. Despise me if I don't. Three important men of this city, pleading in person for him to make me his lieutenant, stood before him hat in hand — and on my word as a man, I know what I'm worth: I deserve a post at least that good. But he, in love with his own pride and his own plans, brushed them off with a long, puffed-up speech horribly stuffed with military jargon, and in the end threw out my backers' case. “Truly,” he says, “I have already chosen my officer.” And who was he? Why, a great mathematician — one Michael Cassio, a Florentine, a man almost damned by a beautiful wife — who has never led a company onto a battlefield, and knows no more about arranging troops for battle than a woman at her spinning wheel — only the theory out of books, which any senator in his civilian robe could lecture on as expertly as he can. Pure chatter, no experience — that's all his soldiering is. But he, sir, got the promotion, and I — whose service the general's own eyes had seen proved at Rhodes, at Cyprus, and on other battlefields, Christian and pagan — must be left with the wind stolen out of my sails, dead in the water, by this bookkeeper, this adder-up of debits and credits. He, if you please, gets to be his lieutenant, and I — God help us — His Moorship's ensign.
RODERIGO. By heaven, I'd rather have been his hangman.

IAGO. Well, there's nothing to be done. It's the curse of the service: promotion goes by recommendation letters and favoritism, and not by the old ladder of seniority, where each number two stood next in line to number one. Now, sir, you judge for yourself whether I'm bound by any fair reason to love the Moor.
RODERIGO. Then I wouldn't serve under him.

IAGO. Oh, sir, don't worry. I serve him so I can serve my own ends against him. We can't all be masters, and not every master can be faithfully followed. You'll notice plenty of dutiful, bowing-and-scraping servants who, in love with their own groveling slavery, wear out their lives, just like their master's donkey, for nothing but their feed — and when they're old, they're dismissed. Such honest fools should be whipped! There are others who, dressed up in the forms and faces of duty, still keep their hearts working for themselves, and, tossing their lords nothing but a show of service, do very well out of them — and when they've lined their coats with money, they serve no master but themselves. These fellows have some spirit, and I declare myself one of them. For, sir, as sure as you are Roderigo, if I were the Moor, I wouldn't want to be Iago. In serving him, I'm only serving myself. Heaven is my judge, I don't do it out of love and duty, but only seem to, for my own private purpose. For when my outward actions put on display the true workings and shape of my heart for all to see, it won't be long before I wear my heart on my sleeve for jackdaws to peck at. I am not what I am.
RODERIGO. What a stroke of luck the thick-lips has in his hands if he can pull this off!

IAGO. Call up her father. Wake him, go after the Moor, poison his joy, denounce him in the streets, stir up her relatives' rage, and though he's living in a rich, fertile paradise, plague him with flies. Though his joy is real joy, throw so many torments and annoyances at it that it loses some of its shine.
RODERIGO. Here's her father's house. I'll shout for him.
IAGO. Do it — with the same terrified tone and ghastly yell as when a fire, started at night through someone's carelessness, is spotted in a crowded city.
RODERIGO. Hey there, Brabantio! Signior Brabantio, hey!
IAGO. Wake up! Hey, Brabantio! Thieves, thieves! Look after your house, your daughter and your moneybags! Thieves, thieves!
[Brabantio appears above at a window.]
BRABANTIO. What's the reason for this terrible racket? What's going on out there?
RODERIGO. Sir, is all your household at home?
IAGO. Are your doors locked?
BRABANTIO. Why? Why do you ask?

IAGO. By God's wounds, sir, you've been robbed! For shame, put on your robe! Your heart is broken, you've lost half your soul. Right now, now, this very minute, an old black ram is mounting your white ewe. Get up, get up! Ring the bell and wake the snoring citizens, or else the devil will make you a grandfather. Get up, I tell you!
BRABANTIO. What, have you gone mad?
RODERIGO. Most honored sir, do you recognize my voice?
BRABANTIO. No. Who are you?
RODERIGO. My name is Roderigo.

BRABANTIO. All the less welcome. I've ordered you not to hang around my door. You've heard me tell you in plain, honest words that my daughter is not for you. And now, like a madman, full of dinner and drinks that have muddled your head, out of drunken, spiteful bravado, you come to shatter my peace.
RODERIGO. Sir, sir, sir —
BRABANTIO. But you can be quite sure that my temper and my rank give me the power to make you regret this bitterly.
RODERIGO. Be patient, good sir.
BRABANTIO. What are you telling me about robbery? This is Venice. My house isn't some lonely farmhouse.
RODERIGO. Most respected Brabantio, I come to you in simple good faith.

IAGO. By God's wounds, sir, you're one of those people who won't serve God just because the devil tells you to. Because we come to do you a favor and you take us for thugs, you'll have your daughter covered by a Barbary stallion; you'll have your grandchildren neighing at you; you'll have racehorses for cousins and Spanish ponies for relatives.
BRABANTIO. What foul-mouthed wretch are you?
IAGO. I'm someone, sir, who has come to tell you that your daughter and the Moor are, right now, making the beast with two backs.
BRABANTIO. You're a villain.
IAGO. And you're — a senator.
BRABANTIO. You'll pay for this. I know you, Roderigo.

RODERIGO. Sir, I'll answer for anything. But I beg you: if it's by your wish and with your wise consent (as I'm partly starting to think it is) that your lovely daughter, at this dead hour of the night, between midnight and morning, has been carried off with no better and no worse escort than a hired servant, a gondolier, into the crude embrace of a lustful Moor — if you know about this and allowed it, then we've done you a bold and insolent wrong. But if you don't know it, my sense of manners tells me you're scolding us unfairly. Don't believe that I've strayed so far from all decency that I'd play games and joke with your honor like this. Your daughter — if you haven't given her permission — I say again, has committed a shocking rebellion, tying her duty, beauty, intelligence and fortune to a vagabond, drifting foreigner here one day and anywhere the next. See for yourself right now: if she's in her room, or anywhere in your house, let the law of the state loose on me for tricking you like this.
BRABANTIO. Strike a light, there! Give me a candle! Wake all my household! This business is not unlike a dream I had; believing it already weighs on me. Light, I tell you, light!
[Exit from above.]

IAGO. Goodbye — I have to leave you. It wouldn't be fitting or healthy for my position to be called as a witness — as I will be if I stay — against the Moor. For I know the state, however much this may chafe him with some reprimand, can't safely dismiss him, because he's been launched, for such loud and pressing reasons, to the Cyprus wars, which are under way right now: to save their souls, they've no one else of his depth and ability to run their campaign. For that reason, though I hate him as much as I hate the pains of hell, yet, since I have to make a living for now, I must hang out a flag and signal of love, which is really nothing but a signal. To be sure of finding him, lead the search party you raise to the Sagittary inn, and I'll be there with him. So, goodbye.
[Exit.]
[Enter Brabantio with Servants and torches.]

BRABANTIO. It's too true a disaster. She's gone, and whatever is left of my now-worthless life is nothing but bitterness. Now, Roderigo, where did you see her? (Oh, unhappy girl!) With the Moor, you say? (Who would ever be a father!) How did you know it was her? (Oh, she deceives me beyond belief!) What did she say to you? Get more candles! Wake all my relatives! Are they married, do you think?
RODERIGO. Honestly, I think they are.

BRABANTIO. Oh, heaven! How did she get out? Oh, treason of my own flesh and blood! Fathers, from now on don't trust what you see your daughters do as a guide to their minds. Aren't there magic spells by which the nature of youth and girlhood can be corrupted? Haven't you read, Roderigo, of some such thing?
RODERIGO. Yes, sir, I certainly have.
BRABANTIO. Wake my brother. Oh, I wish you'd had her! Some of you go one way, some another. Do you know where we can arrest her and the Moor?
RODERIGO. I think I can find him, if you'll gather a strong guard and come along with me.

BRABANTIO. Please lead the way. I'll call at every house; most of them will obey my orders. Get weapons, there! And wake some of the night-watch officers. Onward, good Roderigo. I'll reward you for your trouble.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 2 — Venice. Another street
paragraphs: [Enter Othello, Iago and Attendants with torches.]

IAGO. Though in the business of war I've killed men, I still hold it a matter of deep conscience not to commit premeditated murder. I lack the wickedness that would sometimes serve me well. Nine or ten times I'd thought of jabbing him right here, under the ribs.
OTHELLO. It's better the way it is.

IAGO. No, but he kept running his mouth, and said such foul and provoking things against your honor that with what little godliness I have I could barely keep my hands off him. But please tell me, sir, are you securely married? Be certain of this: that great nobleman is very much loved, and in practice his word carries double weight, as much as the duke's. He'll force a divorce, or pile on you whatever restrictions and penalties the law — with all his power to enforce it — will give him the rope to impose.

OTHELLO. Let him do his worst. The services I've done for this government will outshout his complaints. It isn't yet known — and when I find that boasting is honorable, I'll announce it — that I take my life and being from men of royal rank. And my merits can speak as equals, without taking their hats off, to as proud a fortune as this one I've won. For understand, Iago, if I didn't love the gentle Desdemona, I wouldn't put my free, unsettled, homeless life into confinement and restriction for all the treasure in the sea. But look — what lights are those coming?
IAGO. That's her father, stirred up, with his friends. You'd better go inside.
OTHELLO. Not me. I must be found. My qualities, my rank and my clear conscience will show me as I truly am. Is it them?
IAGO. By two-faced Janus, I don't think so.
[Enter Cassio and Officers with torches.]
OTHELLO. It's the duke's servants, and my lieutenant. May the night be good to you, friends! What's the news?
CASSIO. The duke sends his greetings, general, and he requires you to appear with all possible speed, this very moment.
OTHELLO. What's the matter, do you think?

CASSIO. Something from Cyprus, as far as I can guess. It's an urgent business. The warships have sent a dozen messengers, one after another, this very night, each on the heels of the last, and many of the senators, woken and assembled, are at the duke's already. You've been urgently sent for, and when you weren't to be found at your lodgings, the senate sent out three separate search parties to hunt you down.
OTHELLO. It's good that you're the one who found me. I'll just have a word here in the house and then go with you.
[Exit.]
CASSIO. Ensign, what's he doing here?
IAGO. Well, tonight he's boarded a treasure ship on dry land. If the capture is ruled legal, he's made for life.
CASSIO. I don't understand.
IAGO. He's married.
CASSIO. To whom?
[Enter Othello.]
IAGO. Why, married to — Come, captain, will you go?
OTHELLO. I'm with you.
CASSIO. Here comes another group looking for you.
[Enter Brabantio, Roderigo and Officers with torches and weapons.]
IAGO. It's Brabantio. General, be careful: he comes with bad intentions.
OTHELLO. Hey there, stop where you are!
RODERIGO. Sir, it's the Moor.
BRABANTIO. Get him — the thief!
[They draw on both sides.]
IAGO. You, Roderigo! Come on, sir, I'll take you on.
OTHELLO. Keep up your bright swords, for the dew will rust them. Good sir, your age will command more respect than your weapons.

BRABANTIO. Oh, you foul thief, where have you hidden my daughter? Damned as you are, you've bewitched her! For I'll put it to anyone with common sense (if she weren't bound in chains of magic) whether a girl so gentle, beautiful and happy, so opposed to marriage that she turned away the rich, curly-haired young darlings of our country, would ever — and make herself the laughingstock of everyone — run from her father's care to the soot-black chest of a thing like you — a thing to fear, not to delight in. Let the world judge me if it isn't plain as day that you've worked on her with foul spells, abused her tender youth with drugs or poisons that dull the will. I'll have it argued in court; it's likely, and obvious to anyone who thinks. So I'm arresting you and charging you as a corrupter of society, a practitioner of forbidden and illegal arts. — Seize him. If he resists, overpower him, whatever it costs him.

OTHELLO. Hold your hands, both you on my side and the rest of you. If it were my cue to fight, I'd have known it without anyone prompting me. Where do you want me to go to answer this charge of yours?
BRABANTIO. To prison, until the proper time of law and the regular court session calls you to answer.
OTHELLO. What if I do obey? How would the duke be satisfied with that, when his messengers are here at my side on some urgent business of state, to bring me to him?
OFFICER. It's true, most worthy sir. The duke's in council, and your noble self, I'm sure, has been sent for.

BRABANTIO. What? The duke in council? At this hour of the night? Bring him along. My case is no trivial matter. The duke himself, or any of my fellow senators, can't help but feel this wrong as if it were their own. For if deeds like this can go unpunished, slaves and heathens will end up running our state.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 3 — Venice. A council chamber
paragraphs: [The Duke and Senators sitting at a table; Officers attending.]
DUKE. There's nothing consistent in these reports to make them believable.
FIRST SENATOR. True, they don't match each other; my letters say a hundred and seven war-galleys.
DUKE. And mine say a hundred and forty.

[SECOND SENATOR And mine say two hundred. But though they don't agree on an exact count (since in cases like this, where reports are based on guesswork, the numbers often differ), still they all confirm a Turkish fleet, and one heading for Cyprus.]
DUKE. No, it makes sense enough when you think it through. I won't take false comfort from the mistakes in the numbers, but the main point I do accept as true, and it frightens me.
SAILOR. Hey there! Hey there! Hey there!
OFFICER. A messenger from the war-galleys.
[Enter Sailor.]
DUKE. Now — what's your business?
SAILOR. The Turkish forces are heading for Rhodes; I was told to report that here to the government by Signior Angelo.
DUKE. What do you make of this change?

FIRST SENATOR. This can't be true — not by any test of reason. It's a show, a decoy to make us look the wrong way. When we consider how important Cyprus is to the Turk, and simply remind ourselves again that, just as it matters more to the Turk than Rhodes does, so he can also take it with an easier fight, because it isn't braced for war the same way but completely lacks the defenses that Rhodes is dressed in — if we think about this, we can't believe the Turk is so clumsy as to leave for last what matters to him most, passing up an easy and profitable attack to stir up and risk a danger that gains him nothing.
DUKE. No, you can be sure of it: he's not going for Rhodes.
OFFICER. Here's more news.
[Enter a Messenger.]
MESSENGER. The Ottomans, honored and gracious lords, sailing on a steady course toward the island of Rhodes, have joined up there with a second fleet.
FIRST SENATOR. Yes, just as I thought. How many ships, would you guess?

MESSENGER. About thirty ships. And now they've turned around and retraced their course, openly steering for Cyprus. Signior Montano, your loyal and most courageous servant, sends you this report with his willing respects and begs you to believe him.
DUKE. Then it's certain: they're going for Cyprus. Marcus Luccicos — isn't he in town?
FIRST SENATOR. He's in Florence right now.
DUKE. Write to him in our name; send it off at top, top speed.
FIRST SENATOR. Here comes Brabantio and the brave Moor.
[Enter Brabantio, Othello, Iago, Roderigo and Officers.]
DUKE. Brave Othello, we must put you to work at once against the Ottoman, the enemy of all of us. Brabantio — I didn't see you; welcome, noble sir, we missed your advice and your help tonight.

BRABANTIO. And I missed yours. Your grace, forgive me: it wasn't my office, or any news of state business I heard, that got me out of bed, and the public crisis doesn't grip me; my private grief is like a flood bursting the floodgates, overwhelming everything, so that it gulps down and swallows every other sorrow and is still as huge as ever.
DUKE. Why, what's wrong?
BRABANTIO. My daughter! Oh, my daughter!
[DUKE and SENATORS. Dead?]

BRABANTIO. Yes, to me. She's been deceived, stolen from me, and corrupted by spells and potions bought from quack peddlers; for nature to go so absurdly wrong, in a girl who isn't simple-minded, blind, or lacking her senses, would be impossible without witchcraft.

DUKE. Whoever it is that, by this foul means, has tricked your daughter out of her own self and you out of her — you'll read the law's deadly book yourself, and apply its harshest letter however you see fit, yes, even if my own son were the man you were accusing.
BRABANTIO. I humbly thank your grace. Here's the man: this Moor, who, it now seems, was brought here by your special order on state business.
ALL. We're very sorry to hear it.
DUKE. Othello, what can you say to this in your own defense?
BRABANTIO. Nothing, except that it's true.

OTHELLO. Most potent, grave, and reverend lords, my very noble masters, good men proven by experience: that I have taken away this old man's daughter is absolutely true; it's true, I have married her. The very head and face of my offense — that's how far it goes, no further. I'm rough in how I speak, and barely blessed with the gentle language of peacetime; for since these arms of mine had seven years of strength in them, until about nine months ago, they have spent their most precious effort on the battlefield, among the army tents, and I can say little about this great world beyond what has to do with fighting and battles, and so I won't do my case much credit by speaking for myself. Still, if you'll kindly be patient, I'll tell you a plain, unvarnished tale of the whole course of my love: what drugs, what charms, what spells, and what mighty magic (since that's what I'm charged with) I used in winning his daughter.

BRABANTIO. A girl who was never forward; so calm and quiet in spirit that her own impulses made her blush; and for her — against her nature, her age, her country, her reputation, everything — to fall in love with what she was afraid to look at! It's crippled and badly flawed judgment that would admit such perfection could go so wrong against all the rules of nature; it must be driven to look for the schemes of cunning hell to explain how this happened. So I declare again that with some drugs that work powerfully on the blood, or with some potion bewitched for this purpose, he worked on her.
DUKE. Saying so is no proof, unless there's a fuller and more open test than the flimsy outward look of things and weak likelihoods of everyday assumption that you bring against him.

FIRST SENATOR. But speak, Othello: did you use underhanded and forceful methods to overpower and poison this young girl's affections? Or did it come from asking, and the kind of fair conversation that one soul offers another?

OTHELLO. I beg you, send for the lady at the Sagittary inn, and let her speak about me in front of her father. If her account shows me to be foul, then the trust, the position I hold from you — don't just take them away, but let your sentence fall on my life itself.
DUKE. Bring Desdemona here.
OTHELLO. Ensign, take them there; you know the place best.
[Exeunt Iago and Attendants.]
[And until she comes, as truthfully as I confess the sins of my flesh to heaven, just as honestly I'll lay out for your grave ears how I came to win this lovely lady's love, and she mine.]
DUKE. Tell it, Othello.

OTHELLO. Her father loved me, often invited me over, kept asking me the story of my life, year by year — the battles, sieges, twists of fortune that I've lived through. I went through it all, from my boyhood days right up to the moment he asked me to tell it, and in it I spoke of the most terrible misfortunes, of stirring adventures at sea and on land, of hair's-breadth escapes in the gap of a broken wall with death all around, of being captured by the arrogant enemy and sold into slavery, of being ransomed from it, and how I carried myself through the history of my travels, in which I had occasion to speak of vast caves and empty deserts, rough quarries, rocks, and hills whose peaks touch heaven — that was how it went — and of the cannibals who eat each other, the Anthropophagi, and men whose heads grow beneath their shoulders. Desdemona would lean in earnestly to hear all this. But again and again household chores would call her away, and as soon as she could hurry through them, she'd come back, and with a hungry ear devour everything I said. Noticing this, I once picked a good moment and found a way to draw from her a heartfelt request that I tell the whole story of my wanderings in full, which she had heard only in bits and pieces, never from start to finish. I agreed, and I often drew tears from her when I spoke of some painful blow that I suffered in my youth. When my story was over, she gave me a world of sighs for my trouble. She swore that, truly, it was strange, it was beyond strange; it was pitiful, it was amazingly pitiful. She wished she hadn't heard it, yet she wished that heaven had made her a man like that. She thanked me, and told me that if I had a friend who loved her, I should just teach him how to tell my story, and that would win her. Taking that hint, I spoke up. She loved me for the dangers I had passed, and I loved her because she pitied them. This is the only witchcraft I have used. Here comes the lady. Let her be the witness.
[Enter Desdemona, Iago and Attendants.]
DUKE. I think this story would win my daughter too. Good Brabantio, make the best of this damaged business. Men would rather fight with broken weapons than with their bare hands.

BRABANTIO. Please, hear her speak. If she admits she did half the wooing, may destruction fall on my head if I lay any blame on the man! — Come here, gentle lady: do you see, in all this noble company, who it is you owe the most obedience to?

DESDEMONA. My noble father, I see here that my duty is divided: to you I'm bound for my life and my upbringing; my life and upbringing both teach me how to respect you. You're the one my duty belongs to; until now I've been your daughter. But here's my husband. And just as much duty as my mother showed to you, putting you ahead of her own father, that much I claim the right to declare I owe to the Moor, my husband.

BRABANTIO. God be with you! I'm done. If it please your grace, let's move on to state business. I'd rather adopt a child than father one. — Come here, Moor: I here give you, with all my heart, what I'd keep from you with all my heart if you didn't already have it. — Because of you, my jewel, I'm glad in my soul I have no other child, for your running off would teach me to be a tyrant and chain weights to their legs. — I'm done, my lord.

DUKE. Let me speak as you would, and offer a wise saying that may serve as a stair or step to help these lovers back into your favor: When there's no cure left, our grief is at an end once we see the worst, when just now we still hung on hope. To mourn a misfortune that's past and gone is the surest way to bring a new misfortune on. When fortune takes what can't be kept and saved, patience makes a joke of the injury she gave. The robbed man who smiles steals something back from the thief; he robs himself who spends his time on useless grief.

BRABANTIO. Then let the Turk cheat us out of Cyprus; we haven't lost it as long as we can smile. A man takes a sentence well — a wise saying, or a verdict — if all he has to bear is the easy comfort he hears in it; but a man who, to pay off his grief, must borrow from his poor patience has to bear both the sentence and the sorrow. These sayings, which can taste like sugar or like bitter gall, are strong both ways, so they cut both ways; but words are only words; I never yet heard of a bruised heart being lanced and cured through the ear. I humbly beg you, move on to the business of state.

DUKE. The Turk is heading for Cyprus with an enormous force. Othello, you know the strength of the place better than anyone. And though we have a deputy there whose ability is widely acknowledged, public opinion, which in the end rules what gets done, feels safer with you. So you'll have to put up with dulling the shine of your new happiness with this rougher and more violent expedition.

OTHELLO. That tyrant, habit, most grave senators, has made the hard flint-and-steel bed of war into my softest feather bed, the down sifted three times over. I admit a natural and ready eagerness that I find in hardship, and I will take on this present war against the Ottomans. So, most humbly bowing to your authority, I ask for proper arrangements for my wife, suitable rank, lodging, and an allowance, with such accommodation and attendants as match her upbringing.
DUKE. If you like, let her stay at her father's.
BRABANTIO. I won't have that.
OTHELLO. Nor will I.

DESDEMONA. Nor will I. I wouldn't live there and stir my father into restless, angry thoughts by being always in his sight. Most gracious Duke, lend your favorable ear to what I'm about to explain, and let me find in your voice a charter to help my lack of skill.
DUKE. What do you want, Desdemona?

DESDEMONA. That I loved the Moor enough to live with him, my outright defiance and the way I've stormed my own future can trumpet to the world. My heart has surrendered to my husband's very nature, even to his soldier's trade. I saw Othello's true face in his mind, and to his honors and his courage I dedicated my soul and my fortunes. So, dear lords, if I'm left behind, a useless moth in peacetime, while he goes to war, I'm robbed of the rites I love him for — the rites of love, the rights of a wife — and I'll have to bear a heavy, dragging wait while my dear one is gone. Let me go with him.

OTHELLO. Give her your approval. Heaven be my witness, I don't ask for this to please the taste of my appetite, or to give in to lust — the passions of youth are dead in me — or for my own satisfaction, but to be generous and open to what she wants. And heaven forbid your good souls should think I'll skimp on your serious and important business because she's with me. No — if the light-winged playthings of feathered Cupid ever stitch my eyes shut with lazy lust, as a falconer stitches a hawk's, blinding the faculties that serve my duties, so that my pleasures corrupt and spoil my work, let housewives turn my helmet into a cooking pot, and every shameful, degrading misfortune rise up in arms against my reputation!
DUKE. Let it be as you decide between yourselves, whether she stays or goes. This matter demands haste, and speed must answer it.
FIRST SENATOR. You must leave tonight.
OTHELLO. With all my heart.
DUKE. We'll meet here again at nine in the morning. Othello, leave some officer behind, and he'll bring our commission to you, along with whatever else of rank and authority concerns you.
OTHELLO. If it please your grace, my ensign; he's a man of honesty and trust. I put my wife in his care for the journey, along with anything else your good grace thinks necessary to send after me.
DUKE. So be it. Good night, everyone. And, noble sir, if goodness never lacks a beauty that delights, your son-in-law is far more fair — more beautiful, more bright — than black.
FIRST SENATOR. Farewell, brave Moor. Treat Desdemona well.
BRABANTIO. Keep an eye on her, Moor, if you have eyes to see: she deceived her father, and she may deceive you.
[Exeunt Duke, Senators, Officers, etc.]

OTHELLO. I'd bet my life on her faithfulness! Honest Iago, I must leave my Desdemona in your care. Please, have your wife look after her, and bring them after me at the best opportunity. — Come, Desdemona, I have only an hour to spend with you, for love, for practical matters, and for giving orders. We must do what the times demand.
[Exeunt Othello and Desdemona.]
RODERIGO. Iago —
IAGO. What is it, noble heart?
RODERIGO. What do you think I'll do?
IAGO. Why, go to bed and sleep.
RODERIGO. I'm going to drown myself, right away and with no holding back.
IAGO. If you do, I'll never love you after that. Why, you silly gentleman!
RODERIGO. It's silly to live when living is torture; and besides, we have a doctor's prescription to die when death is our physician.

IAGO. Oh, what villainy! I've looked at the world for four times seven years, and ever since I could tell the difference between a favor and an injury, I've never found a man who knew how to love himself. Before I'd say I'd drown myself for the love of some guinea hen of a tart, I'd trade my humanity with a baboon.
RODERIGO. What should I do? I admit it's shameful to be so infatuated, but it's not in my virtue — my power — to fix it.

IAGO. Virtue! A fig for that! It's up to us whether we're this way or that. Our bodies are gardens, and our wills are the gardeners. So whether we plant nettles or sow lettuce, set out hyssop and weed out thyme, stock the plot with one kind of herb or split it among many, leave it barren through laziness or manure it with hard work — why, the power to shape and correct all this lies in our wills. If the scales of our lives didn't have one pan of reason to balance the other pan of sensuality, the hot blood and baseness of our natures would lead us to the most absurd outcomes. But we have reason to cool our raging impulses, our carnal stings, our unbridled lusts; and I take this thing you call love to be just a cutting or an offshoot of those.
RODERIGO. That can't be.

IAGO. It's nothing but a lust of the blood that the will allows. Come on, be a man. Drown yourself? Drown cats and blind puppies! I've declared myself your friend, and I admit I'm tied to your merits with ropes of everlasting toughness; I could never be more use to you than now. Put money in your purse; follow the army to the wars; disguise your face with a fake beard; I tell you, put money in your purse. It can't be that Desdemona will keep loving the Moor for long — put money in your purse — nor he her. It started violently, and you'll see it split apart just as violently — just put money in your purse. These Moors are changeable in their desires. Fill your purse with money. The food that tastes as sweet to him now as honey-sweet carob pods will soon taste as bitter as bitter-apple. She's bound to swap him for someone young. When she's had her fill of his body, she'll see the mistake she made in choosing him. She has to have a change, she has to. So put money in your purse. If you're set on damning yourself, do it in a more pleasurable way than drowning. Raise all the money you can. If a holy ceremony and a flimsy vow between a wandering, erring barbarian and an over-clever Venetian girl aren't too much for my wits and all the tribe of hell, you'll have her in your bed; so raise money. To hell with drowning yourself! That's completely the wrong road: you'd do better to be hanged for getting what you want than to be drowned and go without her.
RODERIGO. Will you stand firmly by my hopes if I count on how this turns out?

IAGO. You can be sure of me. Go, raise money. I've told you often, and I'll tell you again and again: I hate the Moor. My grievance is rooted in my heart; yours has just as good a reason. Let's join forces in our revenge against him. If you can cuckold him — sleep with his wife — you'll give yourself a pleasure and me some fun. There are many events in the womb of time that will be born. Forward, march! Go, get your money together. We'll talk more about this tomorrow. Goodbye.
RODERIGO. Where shall we meet in the morning?
IAGO. At my lodgings.
RODERIGO. I'll be there with you early.
IAGO. Go on, goodbye. Are you listening, Roderigo?
RODERIGO. What is it?
IAGO. No more talk of drowning, you hear?
RODERIGO. I'm a changed man. I'll sell all my land.
[Exit.]

IAGO. This is how I always turn my fool into my wallet; for I'd be betraying my own hard-won knowledge if I wasted my time with such a brainless bird except for my own fun and profit. I hate the Moor, and people are saying that between my sheets he's done my job as husband. I don't know if it's true, but I, on mere suspicion of that sort, will act as if it were certain. He thinks well of me; that will make my plan work on him all the better. Cassio's a handsome man. Let me see now: to get his job, and to crown my ambition with feathers by a double piece of villainy. How, how? Let's see: after a while, to fill Othello's ear with lies that Cassio is too intimate with his wife. He has the looks and the smooth manner to be suspected — built to make women unfaithful. The Moor has a frank and open nature that thinks men are honest if they only seem so, and he'll be led by the nose as meekly as donkeys are. I've got it. It's conceived. Hell and night must bring this monstrous birth into the world's light.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 1 — A seaport in Cyprus. A Platform
paragraphs: [Enter Montano and two Gentlemen.]
MONTANO. What can you make out at sea from up on the headland?
FIRST GENTLEMAN. Nothing at all. The waves are whipped up mountain-high. Between the sky and the open sea I can't pick out a single sail.

MONTANO. It seems to me the wind has roared loud here on land; a fiercer gust never shook our battlements. If it's been raging like a thug out on the sea, what oak-ribbed hull, with mountains of water crashing down on it, can keep its joints together? What news will we hear of this?

SECOND GENTLEMAN. That the Turkish fleet has been scattered apart. Just go and stand on the foaming shore: the scolded waves seem to hurl themselves up at the clouds; the wind-shaken swell, with its huge and monstrous mane, seems to throw water on the blazing constellation of the Bear and put out its guardian stars that circle the fixed Pole Star. I've never seen such turmoil on the raging sea.
MONTANO. If the Turkish fleet isn't sheltered and tucked into some bay, they're drowned. They can't possibly have ridden this out.
[Enter a third Gentleman.]

THIRD GENTLEMAN. News, lads! Our war is over. This desperate storm has battered the Turks so hard that their plan is crippled. A noble ship from Venice has seen dreadful wreckage and damage across most of their fleet.
MONTANO. What? Is this true?

THIRD GENTLEMAN. The ship has put in here, a Veronese vessel. Michael Cassio, lieutenant to the warlike Moor Othello, has come ashore. The Moor himself is still at sea, and has been given full command here in Cyprus.
MONTANO. I'm glad of it. He's a worthy governor.
THIRD GENTLEMAN. But this same Cassio, though he brings good news about the Turkish losses, still looks worried and prays the Moor is safe, because they were separated by a foul and violent storm.

MONTANO. Heaven grant he is! I've served under him, and the man commands like a complete soldier. Come on, let's go down to the shore, as much to see the ship that's just come in as to strain our eyes looking out for brave Othello, until the sea and the blue sky blur together and we can't tell one from the other.
THIRD GENTLEMAN. Come on, let's do it, because every minute we're expecting more ships to arrive.
[Enter Cassio.]
CASSIO. Thank you, you brave men of this warlike island, for thinking so well of the Moor! Oh, may heaven protect him against the storm, because I lost sight of him on a dangerous sea.
MONTANO. Is his ship a good one?
CASSIO. His ship is sturdily built, and his pilot is known to be highly expert and proven; so my hopes, not so overfed that they sicken and die, stand a good chance of recovery.
[Within.] A sail, a sail, a sail!
[Enter a Messenger.]
CASSIO. What's that noise?
MESSENGER. The town is empty. On the cliff-edge over the sea people stand in rows, and they're shouting “A sail!”
CASSIO. My hopes picture it as the governor's ship.
[A shot.]
SECOND GENTLEMAN. They're firing a salute, a cannon-shot of greeting. Friends, at least.
CASSIO. Please, sir, go out and bring us back the truth about who's arrived.
SECOND GENTLEMAN. I will.
[Exit.]
MONTANO. But, good lieutenant, is your general married?

CASSIO. Very luckily: he has won a young woman who outdoes every description and every wild rumor, who surpasses all the clever flourishes of poets' praise, and who, simply in the natural beauty God gave her, exhausts anyone who tries to capture it.
[Enter second Gentleman.]
[Well now? Who's come in?]
SECOND GENTLEMAN. It's a man called Iago, the general's ensign.

CASSIO. He's had a very quick and lucky voyage. The storms themselves, high seas and howling winds, the jagged rocks and heaped-up sandbanks, traitors lurking underwater to snag the innocent keel, as if they could feel beauty, have set aside their deadly nature and let the divine Desdemona pass safely by.
MONTANO. Who is she?

CASSIO. The one I was talking about, our great captain's captain, left in the care of the bold Iago, whose arrival here is ahead of what we expected by a whole week. Great Jove, protect Othello, and fill his sail with your own powerful breath, so that he may bless this bay with his tall ship, pant with love's quick breaths in Desdemona's arms, rekindle the fire in our burned-out spirits, and bring all Cyprus comfort!
[Enter Desdemona, Iago, Roderigo, and Emilia.]

[Oh, look! The ship's treasure has come ashore! You men of Cyprus, kneel to her. Hail to you, lady! And may the grace of heaven, in front of you, behind you, and on every side, surround you like a wheel!]
DESDEMONA. Thank you, brave Cassio. What news can you give me of my husband?
CASSIO. He hasn't arrived yet, and I know nothing except that he's well and will be here soon.
DESDEMONA. Oh, but I'm afraid — How did you get separated?
[Within.] A sail, a sail!
CASSIO. The great battle between the sea and the skies split us apart. But listen! A sail.
[Guns within.]
SECOND GENTLEMAN. They're firing their salute to the citadel. This one's a friend too.
CASSIO. Go and find out the news.
[Exit Gentleman.]

[Good ensign, you're welcome. [_To Emilia._] Welcome, madam. Don't let it rub your patience raw, good Iago, that I stretch my manners this far — it's my upbringing that gives me this bold show of courtesy.]
[Kissing her.]
IAGO. Sir, if she gave you as much of her lips as she often gives me of her tongue, you'd have had enough.
DESDEMONA. Oh no, she hardly says a word.

IAGO. Honestly, far too many. I always find that out when I want to sleep. Why, in front of your ladyship, I admit, she tucks her tongue away a little inside her heart and scolds me silently in her thoughts.
EMILIA. You've got little reason to say so.

IAGO. Come on, come on. You women are pretty as pictures when you're out in public, loud as jangling bells in your sitting rooms, wildcats in your kitchens, saints when you do harm, devils when someone harms you, idle play-actors at housework, and busy hussies in your beds.
DESDEMONA. Oh, shame on you, you slanderer!
IAGO. No, it's true, or else I'm a heathen Turk. You get up to play, and go to bed to work.
EMILIA. You're not going to write my praises.
IAGO. No, don't let me.
DESDEMONA. What would you write about me, if you had to praise me?
IAGO. Oh, gentle lady, don't make me do it, because I'm nothing if not critical.
DESDEMONA. Come on, try. — Has someone gone down to the harbor?
IAGO. Yes, madam.
DESDEMONA. I'm not cheerful, but I distract myself from what I feel by acting otherwise. — Come on, how would you praise me?

IAGO. I'm working on it, but honestly, my ideas come out of my head the way sticky bird-lime comes off rough wool: it rips out brains and all. But my Muse is in labor, and this is the baby she delivers: If she's fair-skinned and wise, with beauty and brains, she'll use her brains to put her beauty to use.
DESDEMONA. Nicely praised! What if she's dark-skinned and clever?
IAGO. If she's dark, and clever with it, she'll find a white man to fit her darkness, in bed.
DESDEMONA. Worse and worse.
EMILIA. What if she's pretty and foolish?
IAGO. No pretty woman was ever really foolish, because even her folly — her looseness — got her a baby and an heir.
DESDEMONA. These are silly old absurdities for making fools laugh in the pub. What miserable praise have you got for a woman who's ugly and foolish?
IAGO. There's no woman so ugly and foolish with it that she doesn't play the same dirty tricks the pretty, clever ones do.

DESDEMONA. Oh, what heavy ignorance! You praise the worst one best. But what praise could you give a woman who truly deserves it, one who, by the sheer strength of her goodness, could rightly make even malice itself vouch for her?

IAGO. She who was always beautiful and never proud, who could speak whenever she liked and yet was never loud, never lacked money and yet never dressed flashily, held back from what she wanted, even while saying, “Now I could”; she who, when angered, with her revenge within reach, let her grievance rest and sent her displeasure away; she who was never so weak-minded in her wisdom as to swap a cod's head for a salmon's tail — trade a good thing for a worse, or one sex organ for another; she who could think and never reveal her mind, who saw suitors following and never looked behind; she would be a creature, if such a creature ever existed —
DESDEMONA. To do what?
IAGO. To breastfeed fools and keep the accounts of small beer — petty household trivia.
DESDEMONA. Oh, what a lame and feeble ending! — Don't learn anything from him, Emilia, even though he's your husband. — What do you say, Cassio? Isn't he a thoroughly crude and loose-tongued adviser?
CASSIO. He speaks bluntly, madam. You'll enjoy him more as a soldier than as a scholar.

IAGO. He's taking her by the hand. Yes, that's right, whisper. With a web as thin as this I'll catch a fly as big as Cassio. Yes, smile at her, go on. I'll shackle you with your own fine manners. You're right, that's so, indeed. If tricks like these strip you of your lieutenancy, you'd have been better off not kissing your three fingers so often, as you're about to do again, playing the fine gentleman. Very good; nicely kissed, a splendid bow! That's so, indeed. Your fingers to your lips again? I wish they were enema tubes, for your sake!
[Trumpets within.]
[The Moor! I know his trumpet call.]
CASSIO. That's right.
DESDEMONA. Let's go and meet him and welcome him.
CASSIO. Look, here he comes!
[Enter Othello and Attendants.]
OTHELLO. Oh, my beautiful warrior!
DESDEMONA. My dear Othello!

OTHELLO. It amazes me as much as it delights me to find you here ahead of me. Oh, my soul's joy! If every storm is followed by calm like this, let the winds blow until they've woken Death itself! Let the struggling ship climb hills of sea as high as Mount Olympus, and plunge down again as far as hell is from heaven! If I had to die now, now would be the happiest time, because I'm afraid my soul is so completely content that no other joy like this one will follow in my unknown future.
DESDEMONA. Heaven forbid anything but that our love and happiness should grow just as our days add up!

OTHELLO. Amen to that, sweet heavenly powers! I can't say enough about this happiness. It chokes me here; it's too much joy. And may this, and this — these kisses — be the worst discords our hearts ever make!
IAGO. Oh, you're nicely in tune now, but I'll loosen the tuning pegs that make this music, honest as I am.

OTHELLO. Come, let's go to the castle. — News, friends: our war is over, the Turks are drowned. How are my old friends on this island? — Honey, you'll be much welcomed and loved in Cyprus; I've found great affection among them. Oh, my sweet, I'm babbling out of turn, and I'm besotted with my own happiness. — Please, good Iago, go to the bay and unload my chests. Bring the ship's captain to the citadel; he's a good one, and his merit deserves a lot of respect. — Come, Desdemona, once again, how good to meet you in Cyprus.
[Exeunt Othello, Desdemona and Attendants.]

IAGO. Meet me at the harbor right away. Come here. If you've got any courage — and they say even low men, when they're in love, find a nobility in their natures beyond what they were born with — listen to me. The lieutenant is on watch tonight at the guardhouse. First, I have to tell you this: Desdemona is plainly in love with him.
RODERIGO. With him? Why, that's impossible.

IAGO. Put your finger to your lips, like this, and let your soul learn something. Remember how violently she first loved the Moor, just for his bragging and telling her fantastic lies. And will she keep loving him for his chatter? Don't let your sensible heart believe it. Her eye has to be fed. And what pleasure will she get from looking at the devil? When the blood has gone dull after the act of sex, then to fire it up again and give a stuffed appetite a fresh hunger, there has to be good looks, closeness in age, manners and beauty, all of which the Moor lacks. Now, for want of these necessary comforts, her delicate tenderness will feel cheated, she'll begin to feel sick to her stomach, lose her taste for the Moor and loathe him. Nature itself will teach her this and drive her to a second choice. Now, sir, granting this (and it's a very obvious and natural conclusion), who stands higher in line for this piece of luck than Cassio does? A very smooth-talking scoundrel, with no more conscience than it takes to put on a mere show of polite and decent manners, the better to get what he's after with his lecherous, secret, loose desires? Why, no one, why, no one! A slippery and sly scoundrel, a seeker-out of opportunities, who has an eye that can mint and forge chances even when no real chance ever turns up. A devilish scoundrel! Besides, the scoundrel is handsome, young, and has all the qualities that foolish and inexperienced minds go looking for. A complete pest of a scoundrel, and the woman has already picked him out.
RODERIGO. I can't believe that of her; she's full of the most blessed goodness.

IAGO. Blessed, my fig's end — nonsense! The wine she drinks is made of grapes like anyone else's. If she were so blessed, she would never have loved the Moor. Blessed pudding! Didn't you see her fondle the palm of his hand? Didn't you notice that?
RODERIGO. Yes, I did. But that was only courtesy.

IAGO. It was lechery, I swear by this hand. The table of contents and the hidden prologue to a history of lust and dirty thoughts. Their lips came so close their breaths embraced. Villainous thoughts, Roderigo! When these intimacies lead the way, right behind them comes the main event, the physical act, bodies joined as one. Pah! But, sir, let me guide you. I've brought you here from Venice. Stand watch tonight; I'll arrange for you to be given the duty. Cassio doesn't know you. I won't be far from you. Find some way to make Cassio angry, either by talking too loudly, or sneering at his discipline, or any other way you like that the moment makes convenient.
RODERIGO. All right.

IAGO. Sir, he's hot-headed and very quick to anger, and he may well swing his officer's baton at you. Provoke him so he does, because that's all I need to stir up these Cypriots into a riot, and they won't be calmed down properly again except by getting rid of Cassio. That way you'll have a shorter road to what you want, through the means I'll then have to advance you, and the obstacle will be most usefully removed, and without that we'd have no hope of success.
RODERIGO. I'll do it, if I can find any chance.
IAGO. I promise you will. Meet me at the citadel shortly; I have to bring his luggage ashore. Goodbye.
RODERIGO. Goodbye.
[Exit.]

IAGO. That Cassio loves her, I can well believe; that she loves him is likely and very believable. The Moor, even though I can't stand him, has a faithful, loving, noble nature, and I dare say he'll turn out to be a most devoted husband to Desdemona. Now, I love her too, not purely out of lust (though maybe I'm guilty of just as great a sin), but partly to feed my revenge, because I suspect the lustful Moor has leapt into my saddle — into my bed, with my wife. The thought of it gnaws at my guts like a poisonous mineral, and nothing can or will satisfy my soul until I'm even with him, wife for wife, or, if I fail at that, until I at least drive the Moor into a jealousy so strong that reason can't cure it. And to do that, if this worthless Venetian trash, whom I trash — hold back like a hound on a leash — so he won't hunt too fast, holds firm when I urge him on, I'll have our Michael Cassio at my mercy, held like a wrestler by the hip, slander him to the Moor as a crude seducer (because I suspect Cassio has worn my nightcap too — been in my bed), make the Moor thank me, love me, and reward me for making a complete ass of him and plotting against his peace and quiet until he goes mad. It's all here in my head, but still muddled. A villain's plan never shows its true face until it's used.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 2 — A street
paragraphs: [Enter Othello's Herald with a proclamation.]

HERALD. It is the wish of Othello, our noble and brave general, that, now that certain news has arrived reporting the total destruction of the Turkish fleet, every man should celebrate the triumph: some by dancing, some by making bonfires, each man with whatever sport and revelry his rank and taste lead him to. For besides this good news, it is also the celebration of his wedding. That is what he wanted proclaimed. All the kitchens and storerooms are open, and everyone is free to feast from now, five o'clock, until the bell has struck eleven. Heaven bless the island of Cyprus and our noble general Othello!
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 3 — A Hall in the Castle
paragraphs: [Enter Othello, Desdemona, Cassio and Attendants.]
OTHELLO. Good Michael, you take charge of the guard tonight. Let's train ourselves in that honorable self-restraint of not letting the fun outrun good sense.
CASSIO. Iago has his orders about what to do. But all the same, with my own eyes I'll see to it.

OTHELLO. Iago is thoroughly honest. Michael, good night. Tomorrow, as early as you can, I'd like a word with you. Come, my dear love, the bargain is made; its fruits come next; that profit is still to come between me and you. — Good night.
[Exeunt Othello, Desdemona and Attendants.]
[Enter Iago.]
CASSIO. Welcome, Iago. We have to go on watch.

IAGO. Not yet, lieutenant; it isn't ten o'clock yet. Our general sent us off this early out of love for his Desdemona — and we mustn't blame him for that: he hasn't yet spent a night of lovemaking with her, and she's a playmate fit for Jove himself.
CASSIO. She's a truly exquisite lady.
IAGO. And, I'll guarantee, full of play — in bed.
CASSIO. Really, she's a very fresh and delicate creature.
IAGO. What an eye she has! I think it sounds the trumpet for a parley with desire.
CASSIO. An inviting eye, and yet, I think, truly modest.
IAGO. And when she speaks, isn't it a battle alarm calling love to arms?
CASSIO. She really is perfection.
IAGO. Well, happiness to their sheets! Come, lieutenant, I have a jug of wine, and just outside there's a pair of Cypriot gentlemen who'd love to drink a round to the health of black Othello.
CASSIO. Not tonight, good Iago. I have a very poor, unlucky head for drinking. I really wish good manners would invent some other custom for entertaining people.
IAGO. Oh, they're our friends; just one cup. I'll drink the rest for you.
CASSIO. I've had only one cup tonight, and that was cleverly watered down too, and look what a change it's made up here: I have this unlucky weakness, and I don't dare test it with any more.
IAGO. Come on, man! It's a night of celebration. The gentlemen want it.
CASSIO. Where are they?
IAGO. Right here at the door. Please, call them in.
CASSIO. I'll do it, but I don't like it.
[Exit.]

IAGO. If I can just get one more cup into him, on top of what he's already drunk tonight, he'll be as quarrelsome and quick to take offense as my young mistress's lapdog. Now my lovesick fool Roderigo, whom love has turned almost inside out, has been drinking toasts to Desdemona tonight, whole jugfuls, bottoms up; and he's on watch. Three young men of Cyprus, proud and high-spirited, who bristle at the slightest touch on their honor, the very essence of this warlike island — I've made them tipsy tonight with overflowing cups, and they're on watch too. Now, among this flock of drunkards, I'm going to get our Cassio to do something that will offend the island. But here they come. If what follows only proves my dream right, my boat sails freely, with both wind and current behind it.
[Enter Cassio, Montano and Gentlemen; followed by Servant with wine.]
CASSIO. By God, they've already poured me a full round.
MONTANO. Honestly, a small one; no more than a pint, on my word as a soldier.
IAGO. Some wine, hey!
[_And let the drinking-can go clink, clink, And let the drinking-can go clink, clink: A soldier's a man, Oh, man's life's just a span, So why not let a soldier drink._]
[Some wine, boys!]
CASSIO. By God, an excellent song.
IAGO. I learned it in England, where they really are mighty at the mug: your Dane, your German, and your pot-bellied Dutchman — drink, hey! — are nothing compared to your Englishman.
CASSIO. Is your Englishman really such an expert drinker?
IAGO. Why, he easily drinks your Dane dead drunk under the table; he doesn't break a sweat knocking out your German; he has your Dutchman throwing up before the next half-gallon jug can be filled.
CASSIO. To the health of our general!
MONTANO. I'm all for that, lieutenant, and I'll match you drink for drink.
IAGO. Oh, sweet England!
[Sings.]

[_King Stephen was a worthy lord, His trousers cost him just a crown; He thought them sixpence overpriced, And so he called the tailor clown. He was a man of high renown, And you are just of low degree: It's pride that pulls the country down, So wrap your old cloak round you._]
[Some wine, hey!]
CASSIO. By God, this song's even more exquisite than the other one.
IAGO. Do you want to hear it again?
CASSIO. No, because I consider a man who does such things unworthy of his position. Well, God's above everything; and there are souls that must be saved, and there are souls that must not be saved.
IAGO. That's true, good lieutenant.
CASSIO. For my own part — no offense to the general, or to any man of rank — I hope to be saved.
IAGO. And so do I, lieutenant.

CASSIO. Yes, but, if you don't mind, not before me: the lieutenant has to be saved before the ensign. Let's have no more of this; let's get to our duties. Forgive us our sins! Gentlemen, let's see to our business. Don't think, gentlemen, that I'm drunk. This is my ensign; this is my right hand, and this is my left. I'm not drunk now. I can stand well enough, and I speak well enough.
ALL. Very well indeed.
CASSIO. Why, very well then. So you mustn't think that I'm drunk.
[Exit.]
MONTANO. To the gun platform, gentlemen. Come, let's post the watch.

IAGO. You see this fellow who just went out ahead? He's a soldier fit to stand beside Caesar and give orders; and yet just look at his vice: it balances his virtue exactly, like day and night at the equinox, the one as long as the other. It's a pity about him. I'm afraid the trust Othello puts in him, at some unlucky moment when his weakness has hold of him, will shake this island.
MONTANO. But is he often like this?
IAGO. It's always the prelude to his sleep: he'll stay awake while the clock goes round twice if drink doesn't rock him to sleep in his cradle.
MONTANO. It would be good if the general were told about it. Maybe he doesn't see it, or his good nature values the virtues that show in Cassio and overlooks his faults. Isn't that so?
[Enter Roderigo.]
IAGO. What's going on, Roderigo? Please, go after the lieutenant; go.
[Exit Roderigo.]
MONTANO. And it's a great pity that the noble Moor should risk a post as vital as his own second-in-command on a man with an ingrained weakness. It would be the honest thing to tell the Moor so.
IAGO. Not me, not for this whole beautiful island. I love Cassio dearly and would do a lot to cure him of this vice. But listen! What's that noise?
[Cry within: "Help! help!"]
[Enter Cassio, driving in Roderigo.]
CASSIO. By God's wounds, you rogue, you scoundrel!
MONTANO. What's the matter, lieutenant?
CASSIO. A lowlife teach me my duty! I'll beat that rascal till he's criss-crossed like a wicker bottle.
RODERIGO. Beat me?
CASSIO. Are you still yapping, you rogue?
[Striking Roderigo.]
MONTANO. No, good lieutenant; please, sir, hold back your hand.
CASSIO. Let me go, sir, or I'll smash you over the head.
MONTANO. Come on, come on, you're drunk.
CASSIO. Drunk?
[They fight.]
IAGO. Go on, I tell you! Go out and shout that there's a riot.
[Exit Roderigo.]
[No, good lieutenant — for God's sake, gentlemen! Help, hey! — Lieutenant — sir — Montano — sir — Help, gentlemen! This is a fine watch indeed!]
[A bell rings.]
[Who's that ringing the bell? — The devil, hey! The whole town will be up in arms. For God's sake, lieutenant, stop, you'll be disgraced forever.]
[Enter Othello and Attendants.]
OTHELLO. What's the matter here?
MONTANO. By God's wounds, I'm still bleeding; I'm wounded to death.
OTHELLO. Stop, if you value your lives!
IAGO. Stop, hey! Lieutenant — sir — Montano — gentlemen — have you forgotten all sense of your rank and duty? Stop! The general is speaking to you. Stop, stop, for shame!

OTHELLO. Why, what's going on here! How did this start? Have we turned into Turks, and are we doing to ourselves what heaven has stopped the Ottomans from doing to us? For Christian shame, put an end to this savage brawl. The next man who moves to carve someone up to feed his own rage values his soul cheaply: he dies the moment he moves. Silence that dreadful bell; it's frightening the island out of its peace and order. What's the matter, gentlemen? Honest Iago, you look dead with grief; speak: who started this? By your love for me, I order you.

IAGO. I don't know. All friends just now, a moment ago, getting along, and as affectionate as a bride and groom undressing for bed; and then, just now, as if some planet had driven men out of their wits, swords out, and thrusting at each other's chests in bloody combat. I can't tell you how this senseless quarrel began; and I wish I had lost in some glorious battle these legs that brought me here to take part in it!
OTHELLO. How is it, Michael, that you've forgotten yourself like this?
CASSIO. Please, forgive me; I can't speak.

OTHELLO. Worthy Montano, you used to be so well-behaved. The seriousness and composure of your youth have been noticed by the world, and your name is highly praised by the wisest judges. What's the matter, that you rip open your reputation like this and squander your rich good name for the title of a night-time brawler? Give me an answer.

MONTANO. Worthy Othello, I'm dangerously hurt. Your officer, Iago, can tell you — while I save my breath, since speaking hurts me a bit right now — everything I know; and I don't know of anything said or done wrong by me tonight, unless looking after yourself is sometimes a vice, and it's a sin to defend ourselves when violence attacks us.

OTHELLO. Now, by heaven, my blood is starting to overrule my safer guide, my reason, and passion, having clouded my better judgment, is trying to take the lead. By God's wounds, if I move, or just lift this arm, the best of you will go down under my punishment. Let me know how this foul riot began, who started it; and the man proved guilty of this offense, even if he were my twin, born at the same birth, will lose me. What! In a town at war, still unsettled, the people's hearts brimming with fear, to carry on a private, personal quarrel at night, and at the very headquarters and guard post meant to keep us safe? It's monstrous. Iago, who started it?
MONTANO. If, because you're biased by friendship or bound to him as a fellow officer, you tell more or less than the truth, you're no soldier.

IAGO. Don't touch me on so sore a spot. I'd rather have this tongue cut out of my mouth than have it do harm to Michael Cassio. Still, I'm convinced that telling the truth won't wrong him at all. This is how it was, general. Montano and I were talking, when along comes a fellow shouting for help, and Cassio after him with his sword out, determined to use it on him. Sir, this gentleman steps up to Cassio and begs him to stop. I myself chased after the shouting fellow, in case his yelling (as in fact happened) threw the town into panic. He, being fast on his feet, outran me, and I came back all the quicker because I heard the clash and clatter of swords and Cassio swearing loudly, which until tonight I'd never been able to say of him. When I came back (for this all happened quickly) I found them locked together, trading blows and thrusts, just as they were again when you yourself separated them. I can't report any more of this business. But men are men; the best of them sometimes forget themselves. Though Cassio did him some small wrong, as men in a rage will strike those who wish them best, still I'm sure Cassio must have received from the man who ran away some extraordinary insult that he couldn't let pass patiently.
OTHELLO. I know, Iago, your honesty and love are playing this matter down, making it light for Cassio. Cassio, I love you, but you will never again be an officer of mine.
[Enter Desdemona, attended.]
[Look, if my gentle love hasn't been woken up! I'll make an example of you.]
DESDEMONA. What's the matter?
OTHELLO. All's well now, sweetheart; come back to bed. Sir, as for your wounds, I'll be your surgeon myself. Lead him off.
[Montano is led off.]
[Iago, keep a careful watch over the town, and calm down those this vile brawl has upset. Come, Desdemona; it's a soldier's life to have his sweet sleep broken by fighting.]
[Exeunt all but Iago and Cassio.]
IAGO. What, are you hurt, lieutenant?
CASSIO. Yes, beyond any surgeon's help.
IAGO. Why, heaven forbid!
CASSIO. Reputation, reputation, reputation! Oh, I have lost my reputation! I have lost the immortal part of myself, and what's left is animal. My reputation, Iago, my reputation!

IAGO. As I'm an honest man, I thought you'd received some bodily wound; there's more to feel in that than in reputation. Reputation is a useless and utterly false label that others stick on you, often gained without merit and lost without deserving it. You haven't lost any reputation at all, unless you think of yourself as having lost it. Come on, man, there are ways to win the general back: you've only been dismissed in a fit of temper, a punishment more for show than out of malice, just as a man might beat his innocent dog to scare off a menacing lion. Plead with him again, and he's yours.

CASSIO. I'd sooner plead to be despised than deceive so good a commander with such a worthless, drunken and reckless officer. Drunk? And babble like a parrot? And squabble? Swagger? Swear? And rant pompous nonsense at your own shadow? Oh, you invisible spirit of wine, if you have no name to be known by, let's call you devil!
IAGO. Who was the man you chased with your sword? What had he done to you?
CASSIO. I don't know.
IAGO. Is that possible?

CASSIO. I remember a heap of things, but nothing clearly; a quarrel, but not what it was about. Oh God, that men should put an enemy in their mouths to steal away their brains! That we should, with joy, pleasure, partying and cheering, turn ourselves into animals!
IAGO. Well, but you're fine enough now. How did you get over it like this?
CASSIO. The devil Drunkenness has been kind enough to make way for the devil Anger. One flaw shows me another, so that I can thoroughly despise myself.
IAGO. Come on, you're too harsh a moralist. Given the time, the place, and the state this country is in, I sincerely wish this hadn't happened; but since it is what it is, fix it for your own good.

CASSIO. If I ask him for my post back, he'll tell me I'm a drunkard! If I had as many mouths as the Hydra, that answer would shut them all. To be a sensible man one minute, a fool the next, and then an animal! Oh, strange! Every cup too many is cursed, and what's in it is a devil.
IAGO. Come on, come on, good wine is a good, familiar creature, if it's used well. Stop cursing it. And, good lieutenant, I think you think I love you.
CASSIO. I've had good proof of it, sir. — Me, drunk!

IAGO. You, or any man alive, can get drunk some time, man. I'll tell you what you should do. Our general's wife is the general now — I can put it that way because he has devoted and surrendered himself entirely to studying, observing and noting her qualities and graces. Confess everything openly to her. Beg her to help get you your post back. She has such a generous, kind, willing, blessed nature that she thinks it a failing in her goodness not to do more than she's asked. Beg her to put a splint on this broken joint between you and her husband, and — I'll bet my fortune against any stake worth naming — this crack in your friendship will heal stronger than it was before.
CASSIO. You give me good advice.
IAGO. I swear it's given in sincere love and honest kindness.
CASSIO. I truly believe it; and first thing in the morning I'll beg the virtuous Desdemona to take up my case. I'll despair of my future if it's cut short here.
IAGO. You're doing the right thing. Good night, lieutenant; I have to go on watch.
CASSIO. Good night, honest Iago.
[Exit.]

IAGO. And who's this, then, who says I'm playing the villain, when this advice I give is free and honest, reasonable to anyone who thinks it over, and in fact the way to win the Moor back? For it's very easy to get the sympathetic Desdemona to take up any honest request. She's made as generous as the free elements of nature. And then for her to win over the Moor — even if it meant renouncing his baptism, all the seals and symbols of his redemption from sin — his soul is so chained to his love for her that she can make, unmake, do whatever she likes, just as her desire chooses to play god over his weak faculties. How am I a villain, then, to advise Cassio to take this parallel course, one that runs in line with his aim and straight to his own good? The theology of hell! When devils want to promote the blackest sins, they tempt at first with heavenly appearances, as I'm doing now. For while this honest fool begs Desdemona to repair his fortunes, and she pleads hard for him with the Moor, I'll pour this poison into the Moor's ear: that she wants Cassio back to satisfy her body's lust. And the harder she tries to do him good, the more she'll undo her credit with the Moor. So I'll turn her virtue into black pitch, and out of her own goodness make the net that will trap them all.
[Enter Roderigo.]
[What's going on, Roderigo?]

RODERIGO. I'm following along in this hunt not like a hound that does the hunting, but like one that just adds to the barking of the pack. My money's nearly gone; I've been thoroughly beaten up tonight; and I think the upshot will be that I'll get this much experience for my trouble, and so, with no money at all and a little more sense, go back to Venice.

IAGO. How poor are those who have no patience! What wound ever healed except bit by bit? You know we work by cunning, not by witchcraft, and cunning depends on slow-moving time. Isn't it going well? Cassio has beaten you, and you, by that small hurt, have got Cassio fired. Though other plants may flourish in the sun, still the fruit that blossoms first will ripen first. Be patient a while. By the Mass, it's morning; pleasure and action make the hours seem short. Go on back; go to where you're lodged. Go, I tell you; you'll find out more later. No, just go.
[Exit Roderigo.]

[Two things need doing: my wife has to plead for Cassio with her mistress — I'll set her on to it — meanwhile I'll take the Moor aside myself and bring him in at just the moment he can find Cassio pleading with his wife. Yes, that's the way. Don't blunt the plan with sluggishness and delay.]
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 1 — Cyprus. Before the Castle
paragraphs: [Enter Cassio and some Musicians.]
CASSIO. Musicians, play here — I'll pay you for your trouble — something short; and wish the general “Good morning.”
[Music.]
[Enter Clown.]
CLOWN. Why, musicians, have your instruments been to Naples — where the pox eats away noses — that they talk through the nose like this?
FIRST MUSICIAN. What, sir, what?
CLOWN. Tell me, please, are these wind instruments?
FIRST MUSICIAN. Yes, indeed they are, sir.
CLOWN. Oh, thereby hangs a tail — a tale to tell, and a tail behind.
FIRST MUSICIAN. What tale hangs by it, sir?

CLOWN. Why, sir, a tail hangs by many a wind instrument I know — the kind that blows from behind. But, musicians, here's money for you: and the general likes your music so much that he asks you, for love's sake, to make no more noise with it.
FIRST MUSICIAN. Well, sir, we won't.
CLOWN. If you have any music that can't be heard, go at it again. But, as they say, the general doesn't much care to hear music.
FIRST MUSICIAN. We have none like that, sir.
CLOWN. Then pack your pipes back in your bag, because I'm off. Go, vanish into thin air, away!
[Exeunt Musicians.]
CASSIO. Do you hear, my honest friend?
CLOWN. No, I don't hear your honest friend. I hear you.

CASSIO. Please, spare me your wordplay. Here's a small gold coin for you: if the lady who waits on the general's wife is up and about, tell her there's a man called Cassio who begs the small favor of a word with her. Will you do this?
CLOWN. She is up and about, sir; if she'll stir herself over here, I shall endeavor to notify her of it.
CASSIO. Do, my good friend.
[Exit Clown.]
[Enter Iago.]
[Good timing, Iago.]
IAGO. So you haven't been to bed, then?

CASSIO. Why, no. Day had dawned before we parted. I've taken the liberty, Iago, of sending in for your wife. What I want to ask her is that she'll arrange for me to have some access to virtuous Desdemona.
IAGO. I'll send her out to you right away, and I'll find some way to draw the Moor out of the way, so that your conversation and business can go on more freely.
CASSIO. I humbly thank you for it.
[Exit Iago.]
[I never knew even a fellow Florentine more kind and honest.]
[Enter Emilia.]

EMILIA. Good morning, good lieutenant; I'm sorry about your disgrace, but surely all will be well. The general and his wife are talking about it, and she speaks up for you boldly: the Moor answers that the man you wounded is highly respected in Cyprus and very well connected, and that plain good sense left him no choice but to dismiss you; but he swears he loves you, and needs no one else to plead for you but his own affection to seize the first safe opportunity by the forelock and bring you back again.
CASSIO. Still, I beg you, if you think it right, or if it can be arranged, give me the chance of a short conversation with Desdemona alone.
EMILIA. Please, come in. I'll put you somewhere you'll have time to speak what's in your heart freely.
CASSIO. I'm very much in your debt.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 2 — Cyprus. A Room in the Castle
paragraphs: [Enter Othello, Iago and Gentlemen.]
OTHELLO. Iago, give these letters to the ship's pilot, and through him send my respects to the senate. When that's done, I'll be walking along the fortifications; meet me there.
IAGO. Very well, my good lord, I'll do it.
OTHELLO. This fortification, gentlemen — shall we go and look at it?
GENTLEMEN. We'll attend your lordship.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 3 — Cyprus. The Garden of the Castle
paragraphs: [Enter Desdemona, Cassio and Emilia.]
DESDEMONA. You can be sure, good Cassio, I'll do everything in my power on your behalf.
EMILIA. Do, good madam. I'm sure it upsets my husband as much as if the trouble were his own.
DESDEMONA. Oh, he's an honest fellow. Don't you doubt, Cassio, that I'll have my lord and you once again as friendly as you were.
CASSIO. Generous madam, whatever becomes of Michael Cassio, he'll never be anything but your true servant.
DESDEMONA. I know it. Thank you. You love my lord. You've known him long; and you can be quite sure his coolness will keep you no farther away than political caution requires.

CASSIO. Yes, but, lady, that caution may either last so long, or survive on so thin and watery a diet, or keep breeding itself out of chance events, that, with me away and my post filled by someone else, my general will forget my love and service.

DESDEMONA. Don't worry about that. Here, with Emilia as witness, I guarantee you'll get your post back. Believe me, if I swear to a friendship, I'll carry it out to the last clause. My lord will never get any rest; I'll keep him awake till he's tame, like a hawk being trained, and talk till he runs out of patience; his bed will feel like a classroom and his dinner table like a confessional; I'll work Cassio's request into everything he does. So cheer up, Cassio, because your advocate would rather die than give up your case.
[Enter Othello and Iago.]
EMILIA. Madam, here comes my lord.
CASSIO. Madam, I'll say goodbye.
DESDEMONA. Why, stay, and hear me speak up for you.
CASSIO. Madam, not now. I'm very uneasy, in no state to plead my own cause.
DESDEMONA. Well, do as you think best.
[Exit Cassio.]
IAGO. Ha! I don't like that.
OTHELLO. What are you saying?
IAGO. Nothing, my lord; or if — I don't know what.
OTHELLO. Wasn't that Cassio who just left my wife?
IAGO. Cassio, my lord? No, surely, I can't believe that he would sneak off looking so guilty when he saw you coming.
OTHELLO. I really think it was him.
DESDEMONA. Hello, my lord! I've been talking with someone who's come to petition you, a man who's wasting away under your displeasure.
OTHELLO. Who do you mean?

DESDEMONA. Why, your lieutenant, Cassio. My good lord, if I have any charm or power to sway you, accept his apology and make peace with him now; for if he isn't a man who truly loves you, who went wrong out of ignorance and not on purpose, then I'm no judge of an honest face. Please, call him back.
OTHELLO. Did he leave just now?
DESDEMONA. Yes, truly; so humbled that he's left part of his sorrow with me to suffer alongside him. My love, call him back.
OTHELLO. Not now, sweet Desdemona; some other time.
DESDEMONA. But will it be soon?
OTHELLO. All the sooner, sweet, for your sake.
DESDEMONA. Will it be tonight at supper?
OTHELLO. No, not tonight.
DESDEMONA. Tomorrow at midday dinner, then?
OTHELLO. I won't be eating at home; I'm meeting the captains at the citadel.

DESDEMONA. Well then, tomorrow night, or Tuesday morning, or Tuesday noon, or night; or Wednesday morning. Please name the time, but don't let it go past three days. Honestly, he's sorry; and yet his offense, by ordinary reckoning — except that, they say, in wartime they have to make examples of their best men — is hardly even the kind of fault that earns a private scolding. When will he come? Tell me, Othello: I wonder, deep in my soul, what you could ask me that I would refuse, or stand there stammering and dithering over like this. What? Michael Cassio, who came along with you when you were courting me, and who so many times took your side when I spoke critically of you — and I have to go to such lengths to bring him back into favor! Believe me, I could do a lot more —
OTHELLO. Please, no more. Let him come when he wants; I won't refuse you anything.

DESDEMONA. Why, this isn't a favor to me; it's as if I begged you to wear your gloves, or eat nourishing food, or keep yourself warm, or pleaded with you to do something especially good for your own self. No — when I have a request that really means to put your love to the test, it will be heavy, hard to weigh, and difficult, and frightening to grant.
OTHELLO. I won't refuse you anything. In return, I beg you, grant me this: leave me alone to myself for a little while.
DESDEMONA. Would I refuse you? No. Goodbye, my lord.
OTHELLO. Goodbye, my Desdemona. I'll come to you right away.
DESDEMONA. Emilia, come. Be however your whims tell you to be; whatever you are, I'm obedient.
[Exit with Emilia.]
OTHELLO. Wonderful little wretch! Damnation take my soul if I don't love you! And when I stop loving you, chaos will have come again, as before the world was made.
IAGO. My noble lord —
OTHELLO. What are you saying, Iago?
IAGO. Did Michael Cassio, when you were courting my lady, know about your love?
OTHELLO. He did, from first to last. Why do you ask?
IAGO. Just to satisfy a thought of mine; no further harm meant.
OTHELLO. Why, what thought, Iago?
IAGO. I didn't think he'd been acquainted with her.
OTHELLO. Oh yes, and he carried messages between us very often.
IAGO. Indeed?
OTHELLO. “Indeed?” Yes, indeed. Do you see something in that? Isn't he honest?
IAGO. Honest, my lord?
OTHELLO. “Honest?” Yes, honest.
IAGO. My lord, as far as I know.
OTHELLO. What are you thinking?
IAGO. Thinking, my lord?

OTHELLO. “Thinking, my lord?” By heaven, he echoes me, as if there were some monster in his mind too hideous to be shown. You mean something. I heard you say just now that you didn't like that, when Cassio left my wife. What didn't you like? And when I told you he was in my confidence all through my courtship, you cried, “Indeed?” and knitted and puckered up your brow, as if you'd just locked away in your brain some horrible idea. If you love me, show me what you're thinking.
IAGO. My lord, you know I love you.

OTHELLO. I think you do; and because I know you're full of love and honesty, and weigh your words before you give them breath, these pauses of yours frighten me all the more. For in a false, disloyal scoundrel, things like that are just habitual tricks; but in an upright man they're secret signs of feelings he can't hold back, seeping out from the heart.
IAGO. As for Michael Cassio, I'd dare to swear I think he's honest.
OTHELLO. I think so too.
IAGO. Men should be what they seem — or those who aren't, I wish they didn't look like honest men at all!
OTHELLO. Certainly, men should be what they seem.
IAGO. Well then, I think Cassio's an honest man.
OTHELLO. No, there's more to this. Please, tell me what you're really thinking, as you turn it over in your mind, and give the worst of your thoughts the worst of words.

IAGO. Pardon me, my good lord. Though I'm bound to perform every act of duty, I'm not bound to do what even slaves are free to refuse. Speak my thoughts?
