Why, suppose they're vile and false — for where's the palace that foul things don't sometimes break into? Who has a heart so pure that some unclean suspicions don't hold their own little courts there, and sit on the bench alongside honest thoughts?
OTHELLO. Iago, you're betraying your friend — me — if you even think I've been wronged and keep my ear a stranger to your thoughts.

IAGO. I beg you — though maybe I'm wrong, even wicked, in my guess, since, I admit, it's the curse of my nature to pry into wrongdoing, and my suspicious mind invents faults that aren't there — let your wisdom take no notice of me, since my guesses are so unreliable, and don't build yourself trouble out of my random, uncertain observations. It wouldn't be good for your peace of mind or your welfare, nor for my manhood, honesty, or wisdom, to let you know my thoughts.
OTHELLO. What do you mean?

IAGO. A good name in man and woman, my dear lord, is the jewel closest to their souls. Who steals my purse steals trash. It's something, nothing; it was mine, it's his, and has been slave to thousands. But he who filches my good name from me robs me of something that doesn't make him any richer and makes me poor indeed.
OTHELLO. By heaven, I'll know your thoughts.
IAGO. You can't, not even if my heart were in your hand, and you won't, while it's in my keeping.
OTHELLO. Ha?

IAGO. Oh, beware, my lord, of jealousy; it is the green-eyed monster, which mocks the meat it feeds on. The cuckold who knows for sure he's been betrayed, and doesn't love the one who wronged him, lives in bliss; but oh, what damned minutes he counts out, the man who adores, yet doubts; suspects, yet loves intensely!
OTHELLO. Oh, misery!
IAGO. Poor and content is rich, and rich enough; but endless riches are as poor as winter to the man who's always afraid he'll become poor. Good heaven, defend the souls of all my kind from jealousy!

OTHELLO. Why, why do you say this? Do you think I'd make a life of jealousy, forming fresh suspicions every time the moon changes? No. To be in doubt once is to settle the matter once and for all. Trade me for a goat when I turn the business of my soul to such puffed-up, windblown guesses as the ones you're hinting at. It won't make me jealous to say my wife is beautiful, eats well, loves company, speaks freely, sings, plays, and dances well; where there's virtue, these things are all the more virtuous. Nor will I draw from my own lack of merit the smallest fear or doubt that she'll betray me, for she had eyes, and chose me. No, Iago, I'll see before I doubt; when I doubt, get proof; and once there's proof, there's nothing more to it than this: away at once with either love or jealousy!

IAGO. I'm glad of it, for now I'll have reason to show the love and duty I have for you more openly: so, since it's my duty, take this from me. I'm not speaking of proof yet. Watch your wife; observe her closely with Cassio; keep your eyes like this — neither jealous nor too trusting. I wouldn't want your open and noble nature to be cheated because of its own generosity. Watch out. I know the character of our countrywomen well; in Venice they let heaven see the naughty tricks they don't dare show their husbands. Their idea of a clear conscience isn't to leave the deed undone, but to keep it hidden.
OTHELLO. Is that what you say?
IAGO. She deceived her father by marrying you; and when she seemed to tremble and be afraid of your looks, she loved them most.
OTHELLO. So she did.

IAGO. Well, there you are, then. She who, so young, could put on such a show, to blindfold her father's eyes as tight as close-grained oak — he thought it was witchcraft. But I'm very much to blame. I humbly beg your pardon for loving you too much.
OTHELLO. I'm in your debt forever.
IAGO. I see this has dampened your spirits a little.
OTHELLO. Not a bit, not a bit.

IAGO. Believe me, I'm afraid it has. I hope you'll remember that what I've said comes from my love. But I can see you're shaken. I must beg you not to stretch my words into grosser conclusions, or give them a wider reach, than mere suspicion.
OTHELLO. I won't.
IAGO. If you did, my lord, my words would lead to such vile results as my thoughts never aimed at. Cassio's my worthy friend. My lord, I see you're shaken.
OTHELLO. No, not much shaken. I can only believe Desdemona's honest — faithful to me.
IAGO. May she live long that way! And may you live long believing it!
OTHELLO. And yet, when nature strays from its own course —

IAGO. Yes, that's just the point. To be blunt with you, she turned down so many proposed matches with men of her own country, color and class — the kind of match nature always leans toward in everything — ugh! You can smell in a desire like that something rank, a foul mismatch, unnatural thoughts. But forgive me: in making this argument I'm not talking about her specifically, though I may fear that her desire, once it returns to her better judgment, may start comparing you with the men of her own country, and perhaps regret her choice.
OTHELLO. Goodbye, goodbye. If you notice anything more, tell me more. Get your wife to watch her. Leave me, Iago.
IAGO. My lord, I'll go now.
OTHELLO. Why did I marry? This honest fellow, no doubt, sees and knows more, much more, than he's letting on.

IAGO. My lord, I wish I could beg your lordship not to dig into this any further. Leave it to time. Although it's right that Cassio gets his post back, since he certainly fills it with great ability, still, if you'd keep him at arm's length a while, you'll see from that what he's like and how he operates. Notice if your lady pushes hard for his reinstatement with any strong or passionate pleading; that will tell you a lot. In the meantime, let me be thought too meddlesome in my fears (as I have good reason to fear I am) and consider her innocent, I beg your lordship.
OTHELLO. Don't worry about my self-control.
IAGO. Once more, I'll take my leave.
[Exit.]

OTHELLO. This fellow is extraordinarily honest, and with an expert's mind he understands every type of human behavior. If I find she's a wild hawk that won't be tamed, even if the straps that tie her to my wrist were my own dear heartstrings, I'd whistle her away and release her downwind to hunt for herself and take her chances. Maybe because I'm black, and don't have the smooth, charming manners of the ladies' men who frequent women's chambers, or because I've gone down into the valley of old age — though not far — she's gone, I'm deceived, and my only relief must be to loathe her. Oh, the curse of marriage, that we can call these delicate creatures ours and not their desires! I'd rather be a toad and live on the damp air of a dungeon than keep a corner of the thing I love for other men's use. Yet that's the plague of great men: they're less exempt from it than common men. It's a destiny no one can dodge, like death: this forked plague — horns growing from a betrayed husband's forehead — is fated for us even from the moment we're conceived. Here comes Desdemona. If she's unfaithful, oh, then heaven is mocking itself! I won't believe it.
[Enter Desdemona and Emilia.]
DESDEMONA. Hello there, my dear Othello! Your dinner, and the noble islanders you invited, are waiting for you.
OTHELLO. It's my fault.
DESDEMONA. Why are you speaking so weakly? Aren't you well?
OTHELLO. I have a pain here, on my forehead.
DESDEMONA. Honestly, that's from lack of sleep; it'll go away. Just let me tie this tight around it, and within the hour it'll be fine.
OTHELLO. Your handkerchief is too small;
[He puts the handkerchief from him, and she drops it.]
[Leave it. Come, I'll go in with you.]
DESDEMONA. I'm really sorry that you're not feeling well.
[Exeunt Othello and Desdemona.]

EMILIA. I'm glad I've found this handkerchief; it was her first keepsake from the Moor. My unpredictable husband has a hundred times coaxed me to steal it. But she loves the token so much, since the Moor made her swear she'd always keep it, that she carries it with her at all times to kiss and talk to. I'll have the embroidery copied and give it to Iago. What he'll do with it heaven knows, not me; I only want to please his whim.
[Enter Iago.]
IAGO. What's this? What are you doing here alone?
EMILIA. Don't scold me. I have a thing here for you.
IAGO. A thing for me? Your thing's a common thing —
EMILIA. What?
IAGO. — it's common to have a foolish wife.
EMILIA. Oh, is that all? What will you give me now for that particular handkerchief?
IAGO. What handkerchief?
EMILIA. What handkerchief? Why, the one the Moor first gave Desdemona, the one you've so often told me to steal.
IAGO. You've stolen it from her?
EMILIA. No, honestly — she dropped it by accident, and, as luck would have it, I was here and picked it up. Look, here it is.
IAGO. Good girl. Give it to me.
EMILIA. What will you do with it, since you've been so eager to have me swipe it?
IAGO. Why, what's that to you?
EMILIA. If it isn't for some important purpose, give it back to me. Poor lady, she'll go crazy when she finds it missing.
IAGO. Don't let on you know anything about it; I have a use for it. Go on, leave me.
[Exit Emilia.]

[I'll drop this handkerchief in Cassio's lodging and let him find it. Trifles light as air are, to the jealous, confirmations as strong as proofs from holy scripture. This may do something. The Moor is already changing under my poison: dangerous suspicions are by nature poisons; at first they barely taste unpleasant, but once they start working a little on the blood, they burn like sulfur mines. Just as I said.]
[Enter Othello.]
[Look, here he comes. Not opium poppy, nor mandrake, nor all the sleep-inducing syrups in the world will ever dose you back into that sweet sleep that was yours yesterday.]
OTHELLO. Oh! Oh! Unfaithful to me?
IAGO. Why, what's the matter, general? Enough of that.
OTHELLO. Get away! Be gone! You've strapped me on the torture rack. I swear it's better to be cheated on a lot than to know even a little of it.
IAGO. What is it, my lord?

OTHELLO. What sense did I have of the hours she stole for lust? I didn't see it, didn't think it, it didn't hurt me. I slept well the next night, was carefree and merry; I didn't find Cassio's kisses on her lips. A man who's been robbed, if he doesn't miss what was taken — don't let him know it, and he's not robbed at all.
IAGO. I'm sorry to hear this.

OTHELLO. I'd have been happy if the whole army camp, down to the lowest ditch-diggers, had tasted her sweet body, as long as I knew nothing. Oh, now, forever farewell the peaceful mind! Farewell contentment! Farewell the plumed troops and the great wars that turn ambition into a virtue! Oh, farewell, farewell the neighing warhorse and the shrill trumpet, the spirit-stirring drum, the ear-piercing fife, the royal banner, and all the qualities, the pride, pomp and ceremony of glorious war! And oh, you deadly cannons, whose rough throats imitate the dreadful thunder of immortal Jove, farewell! Othello's occupation's gone!
IAGO. Is it possible, my lord?

OTHELLO. Villain, make sure you prove my love's a whore; make sure of it. Give me proof I can see with my own eyes, or, by the worth of man's eternal soul, you'd have been better off born a dog than facing my awakened fury.
IAGO. Has it come to this?
OTHELLO. Make me see it, or at least prove it so well that the proof has no hinge or loop to hang a doubt on — or your life will pay for it!
IAGO. My noble lord —

OTHELLO. If you're slandering her and torturing me, never pray again. Throw away all conscience; pile horror on top of horror; do deeds to make heaven weep and stun the whole earth; for you can add nothing to your damnation greater than that.

IAGO. Oh, grace! Oh, heaven defend me! Are you a man? Do you have a soul, or any sense? Goodbye. Take back my post. — Oh, what a wretched fool I am, to have lived to make my honesty a vice! Oh, monstrous world! Take note, take note, oh world: being straightforward and honest isn't safe. Thank you for this lesson, and from now on I'll love no friend, since love brings on such insults.
OTHELLO. No, wait. You must be honest.
IAGO. I must be wise instead, for honesty's a fool and loses the very thing it works for.

OTHELLO. By the world, I think my wife is faithful, and think she's not. I think that you are honest, and think you're not. I'll have some proof. Her name, which was as fresh as the face of Diana, the chaste goddess, is now grimy and black as my own face. As long as there are ropes or knives, poison or fire, or streams to drown in, I won't put up with this. I wish I were satisfied — that I knew for certain!
IAGO. I see, sir, you're eaten up with passion. I regret that I ever brought it up with you. You want to be satisfied?
OTHELLO. Want to? No — I will be.
IAGO. And you can be. But how? How satisfied, my lord? Would you stand by as a spectator and gawk, mouth hanging open, and watch her being mounted?
OTHELLO. Death and damnation! Oh!

IAGO. It would be a tiresome, hard job, I think, to get them where you could see them like that. Damn them, then, if any mortal eyes but their own ever see them share a pillow! What then? How then? What can I say? Where's your satisfaction? It's impossible for you to see this, even if they were as lecherous as goats, as hot as monkeys, as lustful as wolves in heat, and as crude and stupid as ignorance when it's drunk. But still I say, if suspicion and strong circumstantial evidence that lead straight to the door of truth will satisfy you, you can have that.
OTHELLO. Give me a real, living reason she's unfaithful.

IAGO. I don't like this job, but since I've gone this far into the matter, spurred on by foolish honesty and love, I'll go on. I shared a bed with Cassio recently, and, being bothered by a raging toothache, I couldn't sleep. There's a kind of man so unguarded in spirit that in his sleep he'll mutter about his affairs. Cassio is one of these. In his sleep I heard him say, “Sweet Desdemona, let's be careful, let's hide our love”; and then, sir, he'd grab and squeeze my hand, cry, “Oh, sweet creature!” and then kiss me hard, as if he were pulling up kisses by the roots that grew on my lips, then lay his leg over my thigh, and sigh, and kiss, and then cry, “Cursed fate, that gave you to the Moor!”
OTHELLO. Oh, monstrous! Monstrous!
IAGO. No, this was only his dream.
OTHELLO. But this pointed to a foregone conclusion — something already done. It's a strong reason to suspect, even if it's only a dream.
IAGO. And this may help to thicken other proofs that only show it thinly.
OTHELLO. I'll tear her all to pieces.
IAGO. No, be sensible. We've seen nothing done yet; she may still be faithful. Just tell me this: haven't you sometimes seen a handkerchief embroidered with strawberries in your wife's hand?
OTHELLO. I gave her one like that; it was my first gift.
IAGO. I didn't know that. But today I saw Cassio wipe his beard with a handkerchief like that — I'm sure it was your wife's.
OTHELLO. If it's that one —
IAGO. If it's that one, or any that was hers, it speaks against her, along with the other proofs.

OTHELLO. Oh, if only the scoundrel had forty thousand lives! One is too poor, too weak for my revenge! Now I see it's true. Look here, Iago: all my foolish love I blow away to heaven like this. It's gone. Rise, black vengeance, from your hollow hell! Give up, oh love, your crown and the throne in my heart to tyrant hate! Swell, my heart, with your load, for it's made of the tongues of venomous asps!
IAGO. Still, stay calm.
OTHELLO. Oh, blood, Iago, blood!
IAGO. Patience, I tell you. Perhaps you'll change your mind.

OTHELLO. Never, Iago. Like the Pontic Sea — the Black Sea — whose icy current and unstoppable flow never feels the tide pull back, but keeps rushing on into the Propontic and the Hellespont, just so my bloody thoughts, at their violent pace, will never look back, never ebb into gentle love, until a vast, all-consuming revenge swallows them up. Now, by that marble sky up there, with the proper reverence of a sacred vow I here pledge my word.

IAGO. Don't get up yet. Witness, you ever-burning stars above, you elements that wrap around us on every side, witness that here Iago hands over all the workings of his mind, hands and heart to wronged Othello's service! Let him command, and I'll obey as an act of pity for him, however bloody the business.
[They rise.]

OTHELLO. I welcome your love, not with empty thanks, but by accepting it wholeheartedly, and I'll put you to the test this very moment. Within the next three days let me hear you say that Cassio's not alive.
IAGO. My friend is dead. It's done, because you ask it. But let her live.

OTHELLO. Damn her, the lewd minx! Oh, damn her, damn her! Come, come away with me. I'll go off in private to arm myself with some quick means of death for the beautiful devil. Now you are my lieutenant.
IAGO. I am yours forever.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 4 — Cyprus. Before the Castle
paragraphs: [Enter Desdemona, Emilia and Clown.]
DESDEMONA. You there — do you know where Lieutenant Cassio lies, I mean, where he's staying?
CLOWN. I wouldn't dare say he lies anywhere.
DESDEMONA. Why not, man?
CLOWN. He's a soldier, and if you tell a soldier he lies, you get stabbed for it.
DESDEMONA. Oh, come on. Where is he staying?
CLOWN. If I told you where he's staying, I'd be telling you where I lie — and telling a lie.
DESDEMONA. Can anyone make any sense of this?
CLOWN. I don't know where he's staying, and if I made up a place and said he lies here or he lies there, I'd be lying through my teeth.
DESDEMONA. Can you ask around for him and get yourself educated by what people tell you?
CLOWN. I'll quiz the whole world about him like a preacher with his catechism — that is, I'll ask questions and then answer them myself.
DESDEMONA. Find him and tell him to come here. Tell him I've pleaded with my husband on his behalf, and I hope everything will turn out well.
CLOWN. Doing that is within the range of a man's brains, so I'll give it a try.
[Exit.]
DESDEMONA. Where could I have lost that handkerchief, Emilia?
EMILIA. I don't know, madam.

DESDEMONA. Believe me, I'd rather have lost my purse, stuffed with gold crusado coins. And if my noble Moor weren't so true-minded and free of the kind of meanness that jealous people are made of, this would be enough to set him thinking the worst of me.
EMILIA. Isn't he jealous?
DESDEMONA. Who, him? I think the hot sun where he was born burned all those moody fluids out of him.
EMILIA. Look, here he comes.
[Enter Othello.]
DESDEMONA. I won't let him go now until Cassio has been called back to him. How are you, my lord?
OTHELLO. Well, my good lady. Oh, how hard it is to pretend! How are you, Desdemona?
DESDEMONA. Well, my good lord.
OTHELLO. Give me your hand. This hand is damp, my lady.
DESDEMONA. That's because it hasn't felt old age or known any sorrow yet.

OTHELLO. A damp palm means fruitfulness and a generous — a loose — heart. Hot, hot, and damp. This hand of yours needs to be locked away from freedom, with fasting and prayer, plenty of punishment, and pious exercises; because there's a young, sweating devil in here that usually rebels. It's a good hand, a free one.
DESDEMONA. You're right to say so, because it was that hand that gave away my heart.
OTHELLO. A generous hand. In the old days, people gave their hands in marriage along with their hearts, but in our new coat of arms, it's hands, not hearts.
DESDEMONA. I can't talk about this. Come on now — your promise.
OTHELLO. What promise, sweetheart?
DESDEMONA. I've sent for Cassio to come and speak with you.
OTHELLO. I've got a nasty runny cold that's bothering me. Lend me your handkerchief.
DESDEMONA. Here, my lord.
OTHELLO. The one I gave you.
DESDEMONA. I don't have it with me.
OTHELLO. You don't?
DESDEMONA. No, honestly, my lord.

OTHELLO. That's wrong of you. An Egyptian woman gave that handkerchief to my mother. She was a sorceress, and could almost read people's thoughts. She told my mother that as long as she kept it, it would make her lovable and bring my father completely under the spell of her love. But if she lost it or gave it away, my father would look at her with disgust, and his desire would go hunting after new women. When she was dying, she gave it to me and told me that when fate wanted me to take a wife, I should give it to her. I did. So take care of it — treasure it the way you treasure your own precious eyes. To lose it or give it away would be a disaster like nothing else on earth.
DESDEMONA. Is that possible?

OTHELLO. It's true. There's magic woven into it. A prophetess who had lived long enough in this world to watch the sun complete two hundred yearly circuits — two hundred years — stitched it in a fit of prophetic frenzy. The silkworms that made the silk were holy, and it was dyed in fluid from embalmed bodies, which experts had extracted from virgins' hearts.
DESDEMONA. Really? Is that true?
OTHELLO. Absolutely true. So take good care of it.
DESDEMONA. Then I wish to God I'd never seen it!
OTHELLO. Ha? Why?
DESDEMONA. Why are you talking so jumpily and wildly?
OTHELLO. Is it lost? Is it gone? Speak — is it missing?
DESDEMONA. Heaven help us!
OTHELLO. What did you say?
DESDEMONA. It isn't lost. But what if it were?
OTHELLO. What?
DESDEMONA. I'm telling you it isn't lost.
OTHELLO. Go get it. Let me see it.
DESDEMONA. Well, I could, sir, but I won't right now. This is a trick to distract me from my request. Please, let Cassio be taken back into favor.
OTHELLO. Get me the handkerchief! I fear the worst.
DESDEMONA. Come on, come on. You'll never find a more capable man.
OTHELLO. The handkerchief!
DESDEMONA. Please, talk to me about Cassio.
OTHELLO. The handkerchief!
DESDEMONA. A man who all his life has built his good fortune on your friendship, who's shared dangers with you —
OTHELLO. The handkerchief!
DESDEMONA. Honestly, you're the one in the wrong here.
OTHELLO. Get out of my way!
[Exit.]
EMILIA. And this man isn't jealous?
DESDEMONA. I've never seen him like this before. There must be something magical about this handkerchief. I'm so miserable that I've lost it.

EMILIA. It doesn't take a year or two to show us what a man is really like. They're nothing but stomachs, and we're nothing but food. They gobble us up hungrily, and when they're full, they belch us out.
[Enter Cassio and Iago.]
[Look — Cassio and my husband.]
IAGO. There's no other way; she's the one who has to do it. And look — what luck! Go and beg her.
DESDEMONA. Hello, good Cassio, what news do you have?

CASSIO. Madam, it's my earlier request. I'm begging you: through your good help, let me come back to life once again and have a place in the love of the man I honor wholeheartedly, with every duty my heart can offer. I don't want to be kept waiting. If my offense is so deadly that neither my past service, nor my present regret, nor the good deeds I intend to do in the future can buy me back into his love, then at least knowing that would do me some good. Then I'll dress myself up in a contentment I don't feel, and confine myself to some other way of life, living off whatever charity fortune hands me.

DESDEMONA. Oh, my three-times-gentle Cassio, my pleading for you is out of tune right now. My husband isn't himself. I wouldn't recognize him if his face had changed as much as his mood has. So help me every holy spirit in heaven, I've spoken up for you as well as I possibly could, and I've stood right in the bull's-eye of his anger for speaking so freely! You'll have to be patient for a while. What I can do, I will; and I'll do more for you than I'd dare to do for myself. Let that be enough for you.
IAGO. Is my lord angry?
EMILIA. He's only just left, and he was certainly in a strange, uneasy state.

IAGO. Can he be angry? I've seen the cannon blow his ranks of soldiers into the air and, like the devil, blast his own brother right off his arm — and can he be angry? Then it must be something important. I'll go and find him. There's really something to it if he's angry.
DESDEMONA. Please do.
[Exit Iago.]

[It must be some matter of state — either news from Venice, or some plot not yet hatched that's been uncovered to him here in Cyprus — that's muddied his clear mind. And at times like that men pick fights over little things, even though it's the big things that are bothering them. That's just how it is. If our finger aches, the pain spreads to the rest of our healthy body until we feel it all over. No, we have to remember that men aren't gods, and we can't expect them to be as attentive as they were on the wedding day. Shame on me, Emilia — I was (what a poor soldier I am!) putting him on trial in my heart for his unkindness; but now I see I had bribed the witness to lie, and he's been falsely accused.]
EMILIA. Pray to heaven it's state business, like you think, and not some fantasy or jealous notion about you.
DESDEMONA. Oh, what a terrible day! I never gave him any reason!

EMILIA. But jealous people won't accept that answer. They're not always jealous because there's a reason; they're jealous because they're jealous. Jealousy is a monster that fathers itself and gives birth to itself.
DESDEMONA. Heaven keep that monster out of Othello's mind!
EMILIA. Amen to that, lady.
DESDEMONA. I'll go and find him. Cassio, stay around here. If I find him in the right mood, I'll push your request and do my absolute best to get it granted.
CASSIO. I humbly thank you, my lady.
[Exeunt Desdemona and Emilia.]
[Enter Bianca.]
BIANCA. God save you, Cassio, my friend!
CASSIO. What are you doing away from home? How are you, my beautiful Bianca? Honestly, sweetheart, I was on my way to your house.

BIANCA. And I was on my way to your place, Cassio. What, staying away for a week? Seven days and nights? A hundred and sixty-eight hours? And the hours lovers spend apart drag on a hundred and sixty times longer than the clock's! Oh, what exhausting arithmetic!
CASSIO. Forgive me, Bianca. All this time I've been weighed down with heavy thoughts, but when I have more uninterrupted time, I'll pay off this debt of absence I owe you. Sweet Bianca,
[Giving her Desdemona's handkerchief.]
[copy out this embroidery pattern for me.]
BIANCA. Oh, Cassio, where did this come from? This is a love token from some newer girlfriend. Now I know the reason for the absence I've been feeling. Has it come to this? Well, well.

CASSIO. Oh, stop it, woman! Throw your nasty suspicions back in the devil's teeth, since that's where you got them from. You're jealous now, thinking this is from some mistress as a keepsake. No, I swear it isn't, Bianca.
BIANCA. Well, whose is it?

CASSIO. I don't know either. I found it in my room. I like the embroidery. Before someone asks for it back, which they probably will, I'd like it copied. Take it and do that, and leave me alone for now.
BIANCA. Leave you? Why?
CASSIO. I'm waiting here for the general, and I don't think it would help me — and I don't want it — for him to see me with a woman hanging on me.
BIANCA. Why not, may I ask?
CASSIO. It's not that I don't love you.
BIANCA. It's that you don't love me. Please, walk me part of the way, and tell me if I'll see you early tonight.
CASSIO. I can only walk you a little way, because I have to wait here. But I'll see you soon.
BIANCA. That's fine. I have to put up with how things are.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 1 — Cyprus. Before the Castle
paragraphs: [Enter Othello and Iago.]
IAGO. Is that what you'll think?
OTHELLO. Think what, Iago?
IAGO. What, kissing someone in private?
OTHELLO. A kiss she has no right to give.
IAGO. Or to lie naked in bed with her lover for an hour or more, and not mean any harm?

OTHELLO. Naked in bed, Iago, and not mean any harm? That's putting on a show of goodness just to cheat the devil: people who mean to be virtuous and still do that let the devil tempt their virtue, and they put heaven to the test.
IAGO. As long as they do nothing, it's a small, forgivable slip. But if I give my wife a handkerchief —
OTHELLO. What then?
IAGO. Why then, it's hers, my lord, and since it's hers, she can, I think, give it away to any man she likes.
OTHELLO. She's the guardian of her honor too. Can she give that away?
IAGO. Her honor is something nobody can see; plenty of women seem to have it who don't have it at all. But as for the handkerchief —

OTHELLO. By heaven, I'd have been so glad to forget it. You said — oh, it sweeps back over my memory the way a raven circles over a plague-struck house, a bad omen for everyone inside — that he had my handkerchief.
IAGO. Yes, what about it?
OTHELLO. That's not so good, now.

IAGO. What if I'd told you I'd seen him do you wrong? Or heard him say — since there are scoundrels like that out there who, once they've won a woman over by their own relentless begging, or satisfied some mistress who dotes on them of her own free will, just can't help blabbing about it —
OTHELLO. Has he said anything?
IAGO. He has, my lord, but you can rest assured, nothing more than he'll swear he never said.
OTHELLO. What has he said?
IAGO. Well, that he did — I don't know what he did.
OTHELLO. What? What?
IAGO. Lie —
OTHELLO. With her?
IAGO. With her, on her, whatever you like.

OTHELLO. Lie with her! Lie on her! — We say “lie on her” when people tell lies about her. — Lie with her! That's disgusting. Handkerchief — confessions — handkerchief! Make him confess, and then hang him for his trouble. No — hang him first, and then let him confess. I'm shaking at the thought. My nature wouldn't wrap itself in such a dark, smothering passion unless something real were prompting it. It isn't mere words that shake me like this. Pah! Noses, ears, and lips! Is it possible? — Confess? — Handkerchief? — Oh, devil! —
[Falls in a trance.]

IAGO. Keep working, my medicine, work! This is how gullible fools are caught, and this is exactly how many decent, chaste women, completely innocent, end up disgraced. Hey there! My lord! My lord, I say! Othello!
[Enter Cassio.]
[Hello there, Cassio!]
CASSIO. What's the matter?
IAGO. My lord has collapsed in an epileptic fit. This is his second one. He had one yesterday.
CASSIO. Rub his temples.

IAGO. No, leave him alone; this stupor has to run its course in peace. If it doesn't, he foams at the mouth, and before long breaks out into savage madness. Look, he's stirring: step away for a little while, he'll come round any moment. When he's gone, I need to talk to you about something important.
[Exit Cassio.]
[How are you, general? You haven't hurt your head, have you?]
OTHELLO. Are you making fun of me?
IAGO. Me, mock you? No, by heaven. I only wish you'd take your fate like a man!
OTHELLO. A man with a cuckold's horns is a monster and a beast.
IAGO. Then there are plenty of beasts in a crowded city, and plenty of respectable monsters walking its streets.
OTHELLO. Did he confess it?

IAGO. Good sir, be a man. Remember that every bearded fellow who's married — yoked like an ox — may be pulling the same load as you. There are millions alive right now who lie every night in beds that aren't theirs alone, though they'd swear the beds belong only to them: your case is better. Oh, it's hell's own spite, the devil's supreme joke, to kiss a loose woman in a bed you think is safe and believe she's chaste! No, let me know the truth, and knowing what I am — a cuckold — I'll know what's to become of her.
OTHELLO. Oh, you're wise, that's certain.

IAGO. Stand to one side for a while, and keep yourself within the bounds of patience. While you were lying here, overwhelmed with grief — a passion that doesn't suit a man like you at all — Cassio came by. I got rid of him, gave him a good excuse for your fit, and told him to come back soon and talk with me here, which he promised to do. Just hide yourself away, and watch the sneers, the jeers, and the obvious scorn that live in every corner of his face; because I'll get him to tell the story all over again — where, how, how often, how long ago, and when he has had your wife, and is going to have her again. I'm telling you, just watch his gestures. Now, be patient, or I'll say you're nothing but a bundle of rage and no man at all.
OTHELLO. Do you hear me, Iago? I'll prove very cunning in my patience; but — do you hear? — very bloody.
IAGO. That's not wrong. But keep everything in its proper time. Will you step back?
[Othello withdraws.]

[Now I'll ask Cassio about Bianca, a hussy who, by selling her body's pleasures, buys herself bread and clothes: she's a creature who's crazy about Cassio — since it's a whore's curse to fool many men and be fooled by one. When he hears about her, he can't stop himself from laughing his head off. Here he comes.]
[Enter Cassio.]
[As he smiles, Othello will go mad, and his ignorant jealousy will read poor Cassio's smiles, gestures, and light-hearted manner completely wrong. How are you now, lieutenant?]
CASSIO. All the worse, since you call me by the title whose loss is killing me.
IAGO. Keep working hard on Desdemona, and you're sure to get it back. Now, if this request were up to Bianca, how fast you'd succeed!
CASSIO. Oh, the poor wretch!
OTHELLO. Look how he's laughing already!
IAGO. I never knew a woman to love a man so much.
CASSIO. Oh, the poor thing! I really think she does love me.
OTHELLO. Now he half-heartedly denies it and laughs it off.
IAGO. Do you hear, Cassio?
OTHELLO. Now Iago's urging him to tell it all over again. Go on — well done, well done.
IAGO. She's telling everyone you're going to marry her. Do you intend to?
CASSIO. Ha, ha, ha!
OTHELLO. Celebrating your triumph, Roman? Celebrating, are you?
CASSIO. Me, marry her? What? A prostitute? Please, give my good sense some credit; don't think it's that diseased. Ha, ha, ha!
OTHELLO. So, so, so, so. The one who wins is the one who laughs.
IAGO. Honestly, the word going round is that you'll marry her.
CASSIO. Please, tell me the truth.
IAGO. Call me a real villain if I'm lying.
OTHELLO. Have you branded me and settled my account? Fine.
CASSIO. This is the monkey's own story she's spreading. She's convinced I'll marry her because she loves me and flatters herself, not because I've promised anything.
OTHELLO. Iago's signalling to me. Now he's starting the story.

CASSIO. She was here just now. She follows me everywhere like a ghost. The other day I was talking on the seashore with some Venetians, and along comes the silly plaything and throws herself around my neck like this.
OTHELLO. Crying, “Oh, dear Cassio!” or something like it: his gesture tells me so.
CASSIO. She hangs on me like this, and flops about, and weeps all over me; she tugs and hauls me like this. Ha, ha, ha!
OTHELLO. Now he's telling how she dragged him to my bedroom. Oh, I can see that nose of yours, but not the dog I'll throw it to.
CASSIO. Well, I'll have to stop seeing her.
IAGO. Bless my soul! Look, here she comes.
[Enter Bianca.]
CASSIO. What a polecat — randy and smelly like the rest! Well, a perfumed one, anyway. What do you mean by chasing me around like this?

BIANCA. Let the devil and his mother chase you around! What did you mean by that handkerchief you gave me just now? I was a real fool to take it. I'm supposed to copy the embroidery? A likely piece of work — a likely story — that you found it in your bedroom and don't know who left it there! This is some tart's love-token, and I'm supposed to copy the pattern? There, give it to your cheap little whore. Wherever you got it, I won't copy a stitch of it.
CASSIO. What's wrong, my sweet Bianca? What's wrong, what's wrong?
OTHELLO. By heaven, that must be my handkerchief!
BIANCA. If you'll come to supper tonight, you can. If you won't, come whenever I'm next ready for you — which will be never.
[Exit.]
IAGO. Go after her, go after her.
CASSIO. Honestly, I have to; otherwise she'll make a scene in the street.
IAGO. Will you have supper there?
CASSIO. Yes, I plan to.
IAGO. Well, I may happen to see you, because I'd really like to talk to you.
CASSIO. Please come, will you?
IAGO. Off you go; say no more.
[Exit Cassio.]
OTHELLO. How shall I murder him, Iago?
IAGO. Did you notice how he laughed at his own sin?
OTHELLO. Oh, Iago!
IAGO. And did you see the handkerchief?
OTHELLO. Was that mine?
IAGO. Yours, I swear by this hand: and look how little he values that foolish woman, your wife! She gave it to him, and he's given it to his whore.
OTHELLO. I'd like to take nine years killing him. A fine woman, a beautiful woman, a sweet woman!
IAGO. No, you have to forget that.

OTHELLO. Yes, let her rot, and die, and be damned tonight, because she shall not live. No, my heart has turned to stone; I strike it, and it hurts my hand. Oh, the world doesn't hold a sweeter creature. She could lie beside an emperor and give him orders.
IAGO. No, that's not the way you should think.
OTHELLO. Hang her, I'm only saying what she is. So skilled with her needle, a wonderful musician! Oh, her singing could charm the wildness out of a bear! Such a rich, lively mind and imagination!
IAGO. That makes her all the worse.
OTHELLO. Oh, a thousand, a thousand times worse: and then she has such a gentle nature!
IAGO. Yes, too gentle — too yielding.
OTHELLO. No, that's certain. But yet the pity of it, Iago! Oh, Iago, the pity of it, Iago!
IAGO. If you're so soft on her wickedness, give her a license to sin, because if it doesn't hurt you, it doesn't touch anyone.
OTHELLO. I'll chop her into chunks of meat. Make me a cuckold!
IAGO. Oh, it's vile of her.
OTHELLO. With my own officer!
IAGO. That's even viler.
OTHELLO. Get me some poison, Iago; tonight. I won't argue it out with her, in case her body and beauty weaken my resolve again. Tonight, Iago.
IAGO. Don't do it with poison; strangle her in her bed, the very bed she has contaminated.
OTHELLO. Good, good. The justice of it pleases me. Very good.
IAGO. And as for Cassio, let me take on that job — I'll be his undertaker. You'll hear more by midnight.
OTHELLO. Excellent — very good. What trumpet is that I hear?
[Enter Lodovico, Desdemona and Attendant.]
IAGO. Something from Venice, surely. It's Lodovico, come from the duke. Look, your wife is with him.
LODOVICO. God save you, worthy general!
OTHELLO. With all my heart, sir.
LODOVICO. The duke and senators of Venice send you their greetings.
[Gives him a packet.]
OTHELLO. I kiss the document that carries their wishes.
[Opens the packet and reads.]
DESDEMONA. And what's the news, good cousin Lodovico?
IAGO. I'm very glad to see you, sir. Welcome to Cyprus.
LODOVICO. Thank you. How is Lieutenant Cassio?
IAGO. Alive, sir.
DESDEMONA. Cousin, a painful rift has opened up between him and my husband, but you'll make everything right.
OTHELLO. Are you sure of that?
DESDEMONA. My lord?
OTHELLO. “Be sure not to fail in this, as you would —”
LODOVICO. He wasn't speaking to you; he's absorbed in the letter. Is there a quarrel between my lord and Cassio?
DESDEMONA. A very unhappy one. I'd do a great deal to reconcile them, because of the love I have for Cassio.
OTHELLO. Fire and brimstone!
DESDEMONA. My lord?
OTHELLO. Are you in your right mind?
DESDEMONA. What, is he angry?
LODOVICO. Maybe the letter upset him; because, as I understand it, they're ordering him home and appointing Cassio to govern in his place.
DESDEMONA. Honestly, I'm glad of it.
OTHELLO. Indeed!
DESDEMONA. My lord?
OTHELLO. I'm glad to see you mad enough to say so.
DESDEMONA. Why, sweet Othello?
OTHELLO. Devil!
[Striking her.]
DESDEMONA. I haven't deserved this.
LODOVICO. My lord, nobody in Venice would believe this, even if I swore I saw it: it's going too far. Make it up to her. She's crying.
OTHELLO. Oh, devil, devil! If the earth could breed from a woman's tears, every drop she lets fall would hatch a crocodile, weeping false tears. Get out of my sight!
DESDEMONA. I won't stay and offend you.
[Going.]
LODOVICO. She really is an obedient lady. I beg you, my lord, call her back.
OTHELLO. Mistress!
DESDEMONA. My lord?
OTHELLO. What do you want with her, sir?
LODOVICO. Who, me, my lord?

OTHELLO. Yes, you wanted me to make her turn back. Sir, she can turn, and turn — to any man — and still carry on, and turn again. And she can weep, sir, weep; and she's obedient, as you say, obedient — very obedient. Go on with your crying. About this letter, sir — oh, what a well-acted show of grief! — I'm ordered home. — Get out of here; I'll send for you soon. — Sir, I obey the order, and will return to Venice. — Go on, get out!
[Exit Desdemona.]
[Cassio will take my post. And, sir, tonight I'd like us to have supper together. You're welcome, sir, to Cyprus. Goats and monkeys!]
[Exit.]

LODOVICO. Is this the noble Moor our whole senate calls completely capable in every way? Is this the nature that passion couldn't shake? Whose solid virtue neither the bullet of accident nor the arrow of chance could graze or pierce?
IAGO. He's greatly changed.
LODOVICO. Is his mind sound? Hasn't he gone a bit unhinged?
IAGO. He is what he is. It's not my place to voice my judgment of what he might be. If he isn't what he might be, I wish to heaven he were!
LODOVICO. What, hit his wife?
IAGO. Honestly, that wasn't good; still, I wish I knew that blow would turn out to be the worst of it!
LODOVICO. Is it a habit of his? Or did the letters stir up his blood and create this fault in him fresh?

IAGO. Alas, alas! It wouldn't be honest of me to talk about what I've seen and known. You'll watch him, and his own behavior will reveal him so plainly that I won't need to say a word: just follow him, and see how he carries on.
LODOVICO. I'm sorry I was so wrong about him.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 2 — Cyprus. A Room in the Castle
paragraphs: [Enter Othello and Emilia.]
OTHELLO. So you've seen nothing?
EMILIA. Nor heard anything, nor ever suspected anything.
OTHELLO. Yes, but you've seen Cassio and her together.
EMILIA. But I saw nothing wrong in it, and I heard every single syllable they said to each other.
OTHELLO. What, they never whispered?
EMILIA. Never, my lord.
OTHELLO. Never sent you off somewhere, out of the way?
EMILIA. Never.
OTHELLO. To fetch her fan, her gloves, her mask, or anything?
EMILIA. Never, my lord.
OTHELLO. That's strange.

EMILIA. I'd dare to bet, my lord, that she's faithful, I'd stake my soul on it. If you think otherwise, get rid of that thought; it's deceiving your heart. If some wretch has put this idea in your head, may heaven pay him back with the curse God laid on the serpent! Because if she isn't faithful, chaste and true, then no husband is happy. The purest of wives is as filthy as slander makes her out to be.
OTHELLO. Tell her to come here. Go.
[Exit Emilia.]

[She says plenty. But any brothel-keeper would be a simpleton if she couldn't say as much. This one is a sly whore, a cupboard kept under lock and key, full of vile secrets. And yet she'll kneel and pray. I've seen her do it.]
[Enter Desdemona and Emilia.]
DESDEMONA. My lord, what do you want?
OTHELLO. Please, my chick, come here.
DESDEMONA. What do you wish?
OTHELLO. Let me see your eyes. Look me in the face.
DESDEMONA. What horrible idea is this?
OTHELLO. Do your usual job, madam brothel-keeper: leave the lovers alone to breed, and shut the door. Cough, or clear your throat, if anybody comes. That's your trade, your trade. Go on, hurry up.
[Exit Emilia.]
DESDEMONA. On my knees I ask you, what do your words mean? I can hear the fury in what you say, but not the meaning.
OTHELLO. Why, what are you?
DESDEMONA. Your wife, my lord, your faithful and loyal wife.
OTHELLO. Come on, swear to it, damn yourself, or else, since you look like an angel, the devils themselves might be afraid to grab you. So damn yourself twice over: swear that you're faithful.
DESDEMONA. Heaven truly knows I am.
OTHELLO. Heaven truly knows that you are as false as hell.
DESDEMONA. False to whom, my lord? With whom? How am I false?
OTHELLO. Oh, Desdemona, go! Go! Go away!

DESDEMONA. Oh, what a sad day! Why are you crying? Am I the cause of these tears, my lord? If you happen to suspect that my father had a hand in getting you called back to Venice, don't lay the blame on me. If you've lost his friendship, why, I've lost him too.

OTHELLO. If it had pleased heaven to test me with suffering, if it had rained down every kind of sore and disgrace on my bare head, sunk me in poverty right up to my lips, handed me and my highest hopes over to captivity, I would have found somewhere in my soul a drop of patience. But, oh, to make me a fixed target for this scornful age to point its slow finger at — like a clock hand that never seems to move! Even that I could bear, yes, bear very well. But there, where I have stored away my heart, where I must either live or have no life at all, the spring that my whole stream of life flows from, or else runs dry — to be thrown out of there, or to keep it as a filthy tank for slimy toads to knot together and breed in! — change your complexion at that, Patience, you young, rosy-lipped angel, yes, at that, and look as grim as hell!
DESDEMONA. I hope my noble lord thinks I'm faithful.

OTHELLO. Oh, yes — as faithful as summer flies in a slaughterhouse, that breed the moment they lay their eggs. Oh, you weed, who are so lovely and beautiful, and smell so sweet that my senses ache from you, I wish you had never been born!
DESDEMONA. Oh, what sin have I committed without knowing it?

OTHELLO. Was this fair white paper, this beautiful book, made just to have “whore” written on it? What have you committed? Committed! Oh, you common whore, open to the public! My cheeks would burn like blacksmiths' forges and burn modesty itself down to cinders if I just spoke of what you've done. What have you committed! Heaven holds its nose at it, and the moon shuts its eyes; the lewd, promiscuous wind that kisses everything it meets falls silent in the hollow caves under the earth and refuses to hear it. What have you committed! Shameless whore!
DESDEMONA. By heaven, you're wronging me.
OTHELLO. Aren't you a whore?
DESDEMONA. No, as I am a Christian. If keeping this body of mine for my husband alone, safe from any other foul, unlawful touch, means not being a whore, then I'm not one.
OTHELLO. What, not a whore?
DESDEMONA. No, as I hope to be saved.
OTHELLO. Can that be?
DESDEMONA. Oh, heaven forgive us!
OTHELLO. Then I beg your pardon. I mistook you for that cunning whore of Venice who married Othello. — You, madam,
[Enter Emilia.]
[who have the job opposite to Saint Peter's and guard the gate of hell — you, you, yes, you! We've finished our business. Here's money for your trouble. Please turn the key, and keep our secret.]
[Exit.]
EMILIA. Oh, what is this gentleman imagining? How are you, madam? How are you, my good lady?
DESDEMONA. Honestly, I feel half asleep.
EMILIA. Dear madam, what's the matter with my lord?
DESDEMONA. With whom?
EMILIA. Why, with my lord, madam.
DESDEMONA. Who is your lord?
EMILIA. The one who's yours, sweet lady.
DESDEMONA. I have none. Don't talk to me, Emilia. I can't cry, and I have no answer to give except in tears. Please, tonight, put my wedding sheets on my bed — remember — and call your husband here.
EMILIA. What a change this is!
[Exit.]
DESDEMONA. It's right that I should be treated like this, quite right. What have I done wrong, that he could pin even the smallest suspicion on my slightest fault?
[Enter Iago and Emilia.]
IAGO. What can I do for you, madam? How are you?

DESDEMONA. I can't say. People who teach little children do it with gentle methods and easy lessons. He could have scolded me that way, because, honestly, I'm just a child when it comes to being scolded.
IAGO. What's wrong, lady?
EMILIA. Oh, Iago, my lord has called her whore so many times, thrown such contempt and such heavy insults at her, that no loyal heart could stand it.
DESDEMONA. Am I that name, Iago?
IAGO. What name, fair lady?
DESDEMONA. The one she says my lord called me.
EMILIA. He called her a whore. A drunken beggar wouldn't have thrown such words at his own tart.
IAGO. Why did he do that?
DESDEMONA. I don't know. I'm sure I'm nothing of the kind.
IAGO. Don't cry, don't cry. Oh, what a terrible day!
EMILIA. Did she turn down so many noble suitors, leave her father, her country and her friends, just to be called a whore? Wouldn't that make anyone cry?
DESDEMONA. It's my miserable luck.
IAGO. Curse him for it! How did this delusion come over him?
DESDEMONA. No, heaven only knows.

EMILIA. I'll be hanged if some damned villain, some meddling, smooth-talking rogue, some cheating, lying scoundrel, trying to win himself a promotion, hasn't cooked up this slander. I'll be hanged if not.
IAGO. Nonsense, there's no such man. It's impossible.
DESDEMONA. If there is such a man, may heaven forgive him!

EMILIA. May a hangman's noose forgive him, and hell chew his bones! Why should he call her whore? Who does she spend time with? Where? When? How? What evidence is there? The Moor's been deceived by some utterly villainous crook, some low, notorious crook, some scummy lowlife. Oh heaven, I wish you'd expose such scum, and put a whip in every honest hand to lash the villains naked across the world from the east all the way to the west!
IAGO. Keep your voice down — people will hear.
EMILIA. Oh, curse them! It was some fellow just like that who turned your brain inside out, seams showing, and made you suspect me of sleeping with the Moor.
IAGO. You're a fool. Enough.

DESDEMONA. Oh, Iago, what can I do to win my lord back? Good friend, go to him. For by this light of heaven, I don't know how I lost him. Here I kneel. If my desires ever sinned against his love, either in the course of my thoughts or in actual deeds, or if my eyes, my ears, or any of my senses ever took pleasure in any other man, or if I don't love him still, and always have, and always will — even if he throws me off into a beggar's divorce — love him dearly, then may all comfort abandon me! Unkindness can do a lot, and his unkindness may destroy my life, but it will never stain my love. I can't say “whore”; it fills me with abhorrence now just to speak the word. To do the act that would earn me that title — all the vain riches of the world couldn't make me do it.
IAGO. Please, calm yourself. It's just his mood. The business of the state is upsetting him, and he's taking it out on you.
DESDEMONA. If it were nothing else —
IAGO. That's all it is, I promise you.
[Trumpets within.]
[Listen, the trumpets are calling everyone to supper. The messengers from Venice are waiting to eat. Go in, and don't cry. Everything will be all right.]
[Exeunt Desdemona and Emilia.]
[Enter Roderigo.]
[Hello, Roderigo, what is it?]
RODERIGO. I don't think you're dealing fairly with me.
IAGO. What have I done to make you say that?

RODERIGO. Every day you put me off with some trick, Iago, and now it seems to me you're keeping every opportunity away from me rather than giving me the smallest reason to hope. I really won't put up with it any longer. And I'm not yet ready to swallow quietly what I've already foolishly suffered.
IAGO. Will you listen to me, Roderigo?
RODERIGO. Honestly, I've listened too much, because your words and your actions aren't even related.
IAGO. You're accusing me very unfairly.

RODERIGO. With nothing but the truth. I've spent myself out of all my money. The jewels you've had from me to give to Desdemona would have half-corrupted a nun sworn to chastity. You've told me she received them, and you've brought me back hopes and promises that she'd soon take notice of me and get to know me, but I see none of it.
IAGO. Well, fine, go on, very well.
RODERIGO. “Very well”! “Go on”! I can't go on, man — I can't get at her — and it's not very well. No, I say it's very lousy, and I'm starting to realize I've been made a fool of.
IAGO. Very well.

RODERIGO. I tell you it's not very well. I'm going to make myself known to Desdemona. If she gives me back my jewels, I'll give up my courtship and repent of trying to seduce a married woman. If not, you can be sure I'll demand satisfaction from you.
IAGO. Now you've had your say.
RODERIGO. Yes, and said nothing that I don't solemnly swear I intend to do.

IAGO. Why, now I see you have some spirit in you, and from this very moment I think better of you than I ever did before. Give me your hand, Roderigo. You've raised a very fair objection against me, but still I swear I've dealt with your affair completely straight.
RODERIGO. It hasn't looked that way.

IAGO. I admit it really hasn't looked that way, and your suspicion shows sense and good judgment. But, Roderigo, if you really have in you what I now have more reason than ever to believe you have — I mean determination, courage and bravery — show it tonight. If you don't get to enjoy Desdemona in bed the night after, then kill me by treachery and devise traps to take my life.
RODERIGO. Well, what is it? Is it reasonable, and possible?
IAGO. Sir, special orders have come from Venice appointing Cassio to replace Othello here.
RODERIGO. Is that true? Why, then Othello and Desdemona are going back to Venice.

IAGO. Oh, no. He's going to Mauritania, and taking the fair Desdemona with him, unless his stay here is prolonged by some accident — and nothing could settle that so decisively as the removal of Cassio.
RODERIGO. What do you mean, “removal” of him?
IAGO. Why, making him unable to take Othello's place: knocking his brains out.
RODERIGO. And you want me to do that?

IAGO. Yes, if you dare to do yourself some good and get yourself justice. He's having supper tonight with a tart, and I'll go there to see him. He doesn't know yet about his honorable promotion. If you watch for him leaving there — and I'll arrange for that to happen between twelve and one — you can take him whenever you like. I'll be close by to back up your attack, and between the two of us he'll go down. Come on, don't stand there stunned by it, but come along with me. I'll show you why his death is so necessary that you'll feel duty-bound to deal it to him. It's right in the middle of supper-time now, and the night is wasting away. Get to it.
RODERIGO. I want to hear more reasons for this.
IAGO. And you'll be satisfied.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 3 — Cyprus. Another Room in the Castle
paragraphs: [Enter Othello, Lodovico, Desdemona, Emilia and Attendants.]
LODOVICO. Please, sir, don't trouble yourself any further.
OTHELLO. Oh, forgive me; it will do me good to walk.
LODOVICO. Madam, good night. I humbly thank your ladyship.
DESDEMONA. You are most welcome, your honor.
OTHELLO. Shall we walk, sir? — Oh, Desdemona —
DESDEMONA. My lord?
OTHELLO. Go to bed at once; I'll be back right away. Send your attendant away. See that it's done.
DESDEMONA. I will, my lord.
[Exeunt Othello, Lodovico and Attendants.]
EMILIA. How are things now? He seems gentler than he did.
DESDEMONA. He says he'll be back immediately, he's ordered me to go to bed, and told me to send you away.
EMILIA. Send me away?
DESDEMONA. That was his order. So, good Emilia, give me my nightclothes, and goodbye. We mustn't displease him now.
EMILIA. I wish you'd never set eyes on him!
DESDEMONA. I don't wish that. I love him so much that even his stubbornness, his scolding, his frowns — please, unpin me — have grace and charm in them.
EMILIA. I've put the sheets you asked for on the bed.
DESDEMONA. It doesn't matter. Honestly, how silly our minds are! If I die before you, please wrap my body in one of those same sheets.
EMILIA. Come, come, you're talking nonsense.

DESDEMONA. My mother had a maid called Barbary. She was in love, and the man she loved turned wild and abandoned her. She had a song about “willow” — an old thing, but it told her story, and she died singing it. That song tonight won't leave my mind. It's all I can do not to hang my head over to one side and sing it like poor Barbary. Please, hurry.
EMILIA. Shall I go and get your nightgown?
DESDEMONA. No, unpin me here. This Lodovico is a good-looking man.
EMILIA. A very handsome man.
DESDEMONA. He speaks well.
EMILIA. I know a lady in Venice who would have walked barefoot to Palestine just for one touch of his lower lip.

DESDEMONA. _The poor soul sat sighing beside a sycamore tree, Sing all a green willow. Her hand on her breast and her head on her knee, Sing willow, willow, willow. The fresh streams ran by her and murmured her moans, Sing willow, willow, willow; Her salt tears fell from her and softened the stones —_
[Put these away —]
[Sings.] Sing willow, willow, willow.
[Please hurry. He'll be here soon.]
[Sings.] Sing all a green willow must be my garland. Let nobody blame him — his scorn I approve —
[No, that's not the next line. Listen! Who's that knocking?]
EMILIA. It's the wind.
DESDEMONA. _I called my love a false love; but what did he say then? Sing willow, willow, willow: If I court more women, you'll bed more men._
[So off you go; good night. My eyes are itching; does that mean I'm going to cry?]
EMILIA. It doesn't mean a thing either way.
DESDEMONA. I've heard people say it does. Oh, these men, these men! Do you honestly think — tell me, Emilia — that there are women who cheat on their husbands in such a filthy way?
EMILIA. There are some like that, no question.
DESDEMONA. Would you do such a thing for the whole world?
EMILIA. Why, wouldn't you?
DESDEMONA. No, by this heavenly light!
EMILIA. I wouldn't either, by this heavenly light — I could do it just as well in the dark.
DESDEMONA. Would you do such a thing for the whole world?
EMILIA. The world's a huge thing. It's a big reward for a small sin.
DESDEMONA. Honestly, I don't think you would.

EMILIA. Honestly, I think I would, and undo it once I'd done it. Mind you, I wouldn't do such a thing for a cheap lover's ring, or for lengths of fine linen, or for gowns, petticoats or caps, or any little present; but for the whole world — why, who wouldn't make her husband a cuckold if it made him a king? I'd risk purgatory for that.
DESDEMONA. Curse me if I'd do such a wrong for the whole world.
EMILIA. Why, the wrong is only a wrong in the eyes of the world; and if you got the world for your trouble, it's a wrong in your own world, and you could quickly make it right.
DESDEMONA. I don't believe there is any such woman.

EMILIA. Yes, a dozen; and on top of that, enough to fill up the world they played for with their children. But I do think it's the husbands' fault when wives fall: say they neglect their marital duties and pour what's ours into other women's laps; or else they break out in petty jealousies and lock us up. Or say they hit us, or cut back what they used to give us, out of spite. Why, we have tempers too; and though we can forgive, we can also take revenge. Let husbands know their wives have senses just like them: they see and smell and have a taste for both the sweet and the sour, as husbands do. What is it they're doing when they swap us for other women? Is it for sexual sport? I think it is. And is it desire that drives it? I think it is. Is it weakness that goes astray like this? That too. And don't we have desires, an appetite for sexual sport, and weakness, just as men do? Then let them treat us well; or else let them know the wrongs we do are wrongs they taught us.
DESDEMONA. Good night, good night. Heaven grant me the grace not to learn bad from bad, but to let the bad teach me better!
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 1 — Cyprus. A Street
paragraphs: [Enter Iago and Roderigo.]

IAGO. Here, stand behind this jutting wall. He'll come any moment. Keep your good sword drawn, and drive it all the way in. Quick, quick, don't be afraid; I'll be right at your elbow. This makes us or it ruins us; think about that, and hold your resolve as firm as you can.
RODERIGO. Stay close by; I might botch it.
IAGO. I'm right here, within reach. Be bold, and take your position.
[Retires to a little distance.]
RODERIGO. I'm not very keen on this deed; and yet he's given me convincing reasons. It's only one man gone. Out, my sword; he dies.
[Goes to his stand.]

IAGO. I've rubbed this young pimple almost raw, and now he's angry. Now, whether he kills Cassio, or Cassio kills him, or they kill each other, any way, I win. If Roderigo lives, he'll demand I pay back in full the gold and jewels I swindled out of him as gifts for Desdemona. That can't happen. If Cassio survives, he has a daily beauty in his life that makes me look ugly. And besides, the Moor might expose me to him; that puts me in real danger. No, he must die. But wait — I hear him coming.
[Enter Cassio.]
RODERIGO. I know his walk; it's him. Villain, you die!
[Rushes out, and makes a pass at Cassio.]
CASSIO. That thrust would have been the end of me if my coat weren't tougher than you know. Now I'll test yours.
[Draws, and wounds Roderigo.]
RODERIGO. Oh, I'm killed!
[Iago rushes from his post, cuts Cassio behind in the leg, and exits.]
CASSIO. I'm crippled for life. Help, hey! Murder, murder!
[Falls.]
[Enter Othello.]
OTHELLO. That's Cassio's voice. Iago keeps his word.
RODERIGO. Oh, what a villain I am!
OTHELLO. That's exactly right.
CASSIO. Oh, help, hey! A light! A surgeon!

OTHELLO. It's him. Oh, brave Iago, honest and fair, who feels your friend's wrong so nobly! You teach me what to do. — You little tart, your darling lies dead, and your damned doom is racing toward you. Whore, I'm coming! Those charms of yours, your eyes, are wiped out of my heart; your bed, stained with lust, will be spattered with lust's blood.
[Exit.]
[Enter Lodovico and Gratiano.]
CASSIO. Hey there! No night watch? No one passing by? Murder, murder!
GRATIANO. Something terrible has happened; that cry is dreadful.
CASSIO. Oh, help!
LODOVICO. Listen!
RODERIGO. Oh, wretched villain!
LODOVICO. Two or three are groaning. It's a pitch-dark night. These could be fakes, a trap. Let's not think it safe to go toward the cries without more help.
RODERIGO. Is nobody coming? Then I'll bleed to death.
[Enter Iago with a light.]
LODOVICO. Listen!
GRATIANO. Here comes someone in his shirtsleeves, with a light and weapons.
IAGO. Who's there? Who's making this noise, shouting murder?
LODOVICO. We don't know.
IAGO. Didn't you hear someone cry out?
CASSIO. Here, here! For heaven's sake, help me!
IAGO. What's the matter?
GRATIANO. This is Othello's ensign, if I'm not mistaken.
LODOVICO. The same, indeed; a very brave fellow.
IAGO. Who are you there, crying out so painfully?
CASSIO. Iago? Oh, I'm ruined, destroyed by villains! Give me some help.
IAGO. Oh, no, lieutenant! What villains did this?
CASSIO. I think one of them is somewhere near here and can't get away.
IAGO. Oh, treacherous villains! Who are you there? Come over and give us some help.
RODERIGO. Oh, help me here!
CASSIO. That's one of them.
IAGO. Oh, murdering scum! Oh, villain!
[Stabs Roderigo.]
RODERIGO. Oh, damned Iago! Oh, inhuman dog!
IAGO. Killing men in the dark! Where are these bloody thieves? How silent this town is! Hey! Murder! Murder! Who are you? Are you for good or evil?
LODOVICO. Judge us by how we prove ourselves.
IAGO. Signior Lodovico?
LODOVICO. That's me, sir.
IAGO. I beg your pardon. Here's Cassio, wounded by villains.
GRATIANO. Cassio!
IAGO. How are you, brother?
CASSIO. My leg is cut in two.
IAGO. Why, heaven forbid! A light, gentlemen; I'll bandage it with my shirt.
[Enter Bianca.]
BIANCA. What's the matter, hey? Who was that crying out?
IAGO. Who was that crying out?
BIANCA. Oh, my dear Cassio, my sweet Cassio! Oh, Cassio, Cassio, Cassio!
IAGO. Oh, you notorious whore! Cassio, can you guess who it was that cut you up like this?
CASSIO. No.
GRATIANO. I'm sorry to find you like this; I've been looking for you.
IAGO. Give me a garter. There. — Oh, for a stretcher-chair to carry him gently away from here!
BIANCA. Oh no, he's fainting! Oh, Cassio, Cassio, Cassio!

IAGO. Gentlemen, all of you, I suspect this piece of trash had a part in this attack. Hold on a little, good Cassio. Come, come; give me a light. Do we know this face or not? Oh no, my friend and my dear countryman, Roderigo? No. Yes, it is; oh, heaven! Roderigo.
GRATIANO. What, Roderigo of Venice?
IAGO. The very one, sir. Did you know him?
GRATIANO. Know him? Yes.
IAGO. Signior Gratiano? I humbly beg your pardon. These bloody events must excuse my bad manners in ignoring you.
GRATIANO. I'm glad to see you.
IAGO. How are you, Cassio? Oh, a chair, a chair!
GRATIANO. Roderigo!
IAGO. It's him, him, it's him.
[A chair brought in.]

[Oh, good work; the chair. Some good man carry him carefully away from here; I'll fetch the general's surgeon. [_To Bianca_] As for you, madam, spare yourself the trouble. The man lying dead here, Cassio, was my dear friend. What bad blood was there between you?]
CASSIO. None in the world. I don't even know the man.
IAGO. What, are you turning pale? — Oh, get him out of the open air.
[Cassio and Roderigo are borne off.]

[Stay here, good gentlemen. — Are you pale, madam? Do you see the terror in her eyes? No, if you stare like that, we'll hear more soon enough. Look at her closely. Please, look at her. Do you see, gentlemen? Yes, guilt will speak out even if tongues went out of use.]
[Enter Emilia.]
EMILIA. Oh, what's the matter? What's the matter, husband?
IAGO. Cassio was attacked here in the dark by Roderigo and some others who've escaped. He's nearly dead, and Roderigo is dead.
EMILIA. Oh, poor gentleman! Oh, poor Cassio!
IAGO. This is what whoring gets you. Please, Emilia, go and find out from Cassio where he had supper tonight. What, does that make you shake?
BIANCA. He had supper at my house, but that's not why I'm shaking.
IAGO. Oh, did he? I order you to come with me.
EMILIA. Shame, shame on you, you whore!
BIANCA. I'm no whore; I live a life as decent as yours, you who insult me like this.
EMILIA. As mine? Ugh! Shame on you!

IAGO. Kind gentlemen, let's go and see poor Cassio's wounds dressed. Come, madam, you'll have to tell us a different story. Emilia, run to the citadel and tell my lord and lady what has happened. Will you go on ahead? This is the night that either makes me or ruins me completely.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 2 — Cyprus. A Bedchamber in the castle
paragraphs: [Desdemona in bed asleep; a light burning.]
[Enter Othello.]

OTHELLO. It's the cause, it's the cause, my soul; I won't name it to you, you pure, chaste stars! It's the cause. Still, I won't spill her blood, or scar that skin of hers, whiter than snow and smooth as the alabaster of a statue on a tomb. And yet she has to die, or she'll deceive more men. Put out the light, and then put out the light — her life: if I snuff you out, you flaming candle that serves me, I can bring your earlier light back again if I change my mind. But once your light is out, you most intricate masterpiece of nature at her best, I don't know where to find the heavenly fire Prometheus stole that could relight you. Once I've picked your rose, I can't make it live and grow again; it's bound to wither. I'll smell it while it's still on the bush.
[Kissing her.]

[Oh, sweet-scented breath, that almost talks Justice into breaking her sword! One more, one more. Be like this when you're dead, and I'll kill you and love you afterward. One more, and this is the last. Nothing so sweet was ever so deadly. I have to cry, but these are cruel tears. This grief is like God's: it punishes where it loves. She's waking.]
DESDEMONA. Who's there? Othello?
OTHELLO. Yes, Desdemona.
DESDEMONA. Are you coming to bed, my lord?
OTHELLO. Have you said your prayers tonight, Desdemona?
DESDEMONA. Yes, my lord.
OTHELLO. If you can think of any sin you've committed that isn't yet forgiven by heaven and God's grace, pray for pardon right now.
DESDEMONA. Oh no, my lord, what can you mean by that?
OTHELLO. Well, do it, and keep it short. I'll walk over here. I wouldn't want to kill your spirit while it's unprepared — no, heaven forbid! I wouldn't kill your soul.
DESDEMONA. Are you talking about killing?
OTHELLO. Yes, I am.
DESDEMONA. Then heaven have mercy on me!
OTHELLO. Amen to that, with all my heart!
DESDEMONA. If you say that, I hope you won't kill me.
OTHELLO. Hmm!
DESDEMONA. And still I'm afraid of you, because you're deadly when your eyes roll wildly like that. Why I should be afraid I don't know, since I know I've done nothing wrong — and yet I feel afraid.
OTHELLO. Think about your sins.
DESDEMONA. The only ones I have are the love I feel for you.
OTHELLO. Yes, and that's why you die.

DESDEMONA. It's an unnatural death that kills someone for loving. Oh, why are you biting your lower lip like that? Some murderous rage is shaking your whole body. These are bad omens; but still I hope, I hope, they're not aimed at me.
OTHELLO. Quiet, and keep still!
DESDEMONA. I will. What's wrong?
OTHELLO. That handkerchief I loved so much and gave you, you gave to Cassio.
DESDEMONA. No, I swear by my life and soul! Send for the man and ask him.
OTHELLO. Sweet soul, be careful, be careful not to swear falsely — you're on your deathbed.
DESDEMONA. Yes — but not to die yet.

OTHELLO. Yes, right now. So confess your sin openly, because denying each charge under oath, one by one, can't remove or strangle the powerful belief I'm groaning with, like a woman in labor. You're going to die.
DESDEMONA. Then Lord have mercy on me!
OTHELLO. I say amen.

DESDEMONA. And may you have mercy too! I never once wronged you in my life, and never loved Cassio except with the ordinary love that heaven allows me to feel for anyone. I never gave him any love-token.

OTHELLO. By heaven, I saw my handkerchief in his hand. Oh, lying, perjured woman, you turn my heart to stone and make me call what I mean to do a murder, when I thought it was a sacrifice. I saw the handkerchief.
DESDEMONA. Then he found it. I never gave it to him. Send for him to come here. Let him tell the truth.
OTHELLO. He has confessed.
DESDEMONA. Confessed what, my lord?
OTHELLO. That he has had you.
DESDEMONA. What? Unlawfully?
OTHELLO. Yes.
DESDEMONA. He won't say that.
OTHELLO. No, his mouth has been shut for good. Honest Iago has seen to it.
DESDEMONA. Oh, my fear tells me what that means! What, is he dead?
OTHELLO. If every hair on his head had been a life, my huge revenge would have had appetite enough to devour them all.
DESDEMONA. Oh no, he's been betrayed, and I'm ruined!
OTHELLO. Get away, you whore! Are you crying for him to my face?
DESDEMONA. Oh, banish me, my lord, but don't kill me!
OTHELLO. Down, whore!
DESDEMONA. Kill me tomorrow — let me live tonight!
OTHELLO. No — if you struggle —
DESDEMONA. Just half an hour!
OTHELLO. Now that it's under way, there's no stopping.
DESDEMONA. Just while I say one prayer!
OTHELLO. It's too late.
[Smothers her.]
EMILIA. My lord, my lord! Are you there? My lord, my lord!
OTHELLO. What's that noise? Not dead? Not quite dead yet? I may be cruel, but I'm still merciful; I wouldn't want you to linger in your pain. Like this. Like this.
EMILIA. Are you there? My lord, my lord!
OTHELLO. Who's there?
EMILIA. Oh, my good lord, I need to talk to you!

OTHELLO. Yes. — It's Emilia. — Just a moment. — She's dead. Emilia's probably coming to tell me Cassio's dead; there was a lot of noise out there. — Ha! Not moving anymore? Silent as the grave. Should I let her in? Would that be wise? I think she's moving again. No. What's the best thing to do? If she comes in, she's sure to speak to my wife. My wife! My wife! What wife? I have no wife. Oh, unbearable! Oh, heavy, awful hour! I feel there should be a huge eclipse right now of the sun and moon together, and the terrified earth should gape open in an earthquake at this change.
EMILIA. I'm begging you, let me speak with you — oh, my good lord!
OTHELLO. I'd forgotten you. Oh, come in, Emilia. Wait, just a moment; let me draw the bed-curtains. Where are you?
[Unlocks the door.]
[Enter Emilia.]
[What's the matter with you now?]
EMILIA. Oh, my good lord, there's been foul murder done out there!
OTHELLO. What, just now?
EMILIA. Just now, my lord.
OTHELLO. It's the moon, straying off her proper course: she comes closer to the earth than she used to and drives men mad — lunatic.
EMILIA. Cassio, my lord, has killed a young Venetian named Roderigo.
OTHELLO. Roderigo killed? And Cassio killed?
EMILIA. No, Cassio isn't killed.
OTHELLO. Cassio not killed! Then the murder's out of tune, and my sweet revenge turns into a harsh, jarring note.
DESDEMONA. Oh, wrongly, wrongly murdered!
EMILIA. Oh no, what cry was that?
OTHELLO. That? What?
EMILIA. Oh no, oh no! That was my lady's voice. Help! Help, somebody! Help! Oh, lady, speak again! Sweet Desdemona! Oh, sweet mistress, speak!
DESDEMONA. I'm dying an innocent death.
EMILIA. Oh, who has done this?
DESDEMONA. Nobody. I did it myself. Goodbye. Give my love to my kind husband. Oh, goodbye!
[She dies.]
OTHELLO. Why, how could she have been murdered?
EMILIA. Oh, who knows?
OTHELLO. You heard her say it herself: it wasn't me.
EMILIA. She said so. I'll have to tell the truth.
OTHELLO. She's gone to burning hell like the liar she is. It was me who killed her.
EMILIA. Oh, then she's all the more an angel, and you're all the blacker a devil!
OTHELLO. She turned to lust and wickedness, and she was a whore.
EMILIA. You're slandering her, and you're a devil.
OTHELLO. She was as faithless as water — slippery, never staying put.
EMILIA. You're as reckless as fire to say that she was faithless. Oh, she was true as heaven!

OTHELLO. Cassio was mounting her; ask your husband if you don't believe me. Oh, I'd be damned to the lowest depths of hell if I hadn't had solid grounds to go this far. Your husband knew all about it.
EMILIA. My husband?
OTHELLO. Your husband.
EMILIA. That she was unfaithful to her marriage?
OTHELLO. Yes, with Cassio. Listen — if she had been faithful, even if heaven had made me another world like this one out of a single, flawless chrysolite gem, I wouldn't have traded her for it.
EMILIA. My husband?
OTHELLO. Yes, he was the first to tell me. He's an honest man, and he hates the slime that clings to filthy deeds.
EMILIA. My husband?
OTHELLO. Why keep repeating it, woman? I said your husband.
EMILIA. Oh, mistress, villainy has made a mockery of love! My husband says that she was unfaithful?
OTHELLO. Him, woman. I said your husband. Do you understand the word? My friend, your husband, honest, honest Iago.
EMILIA. If he says that, may his poisonous soul rot away a tiny bit each day! He's lying to the core. She was too much in love with the filthy bargain she made — you.
OTHELLO. Ha!
EMILIA. Do your worst. This deed of yours deserves heaven no more than you deserved her.
OTHELLO. You'd better keep quiet.

EMILIA. You don't have half as much power to hurt me as I have strength to bear the hurt. Oh, you dupe! You idiot! As ignorant as dirt! You've done a deed — I don't care about your sword — I'll expose you, even if I lost twenty lives for it. Help! Help, somebody! Help! The Moor has killed my mistress! Murder! Murder!
[Enter Montano, Gratiano and Iago.]
MONTANO. What's the matter? What's going on, general?
EMILIA. Oh, you've come, Iago? You've done a fine job, if men are blaming their murders on you.
GRATIANO. What's the matter?

EMILIA. Prove this villain wrong, if you're any kind of man. He says you told him his wife was unfaithful. I know you didn't — you're not that much of a villain. Speak, because my heart's about to burst.
IAGO. I told him what I thought, and told him nothing more than what he found for himself to be believable and true.
EMILIA. But did you ever tell him she was unfaithful?
IAGO. I did.
EMILIA. You told a lie, a hateful, damned lie; I swear on my soul, a lie, a wicked lie. She, unfaithful with Cassio? Did you say with Cassio?
IAGO. With Cassio, woman. Come on — put a spell on that tongue and keep it quiet.
EMILIA. I will not hold my tongue; it's my duty to speak. My mistress lies here murdered in her bed.
ALL. Oh, heaven forbid!
EMILIA. And your stories are what drove him to the murder.
OTHELLO. No, don't stare, gentlemen; it's true, all right.
GRATIANO. It's a strange truth.
MONTANO. Oh, monstrous deed!
EMILIA. Villainy, villainy, villainy! When I think about it — I think I can smell it — oh, villainy! I suspected it back then. I'll kill myself with grief. Oh, villainy, villainy!
IAGO. What, are you crazy? I order you, go home.
EMILIA. Good gentlemen, give me permission to speak. It's right for me to obey him, but not now. Maybe, Iago, I'll never go home again.
OTHELLO. Oh! Oh! Oh!
[Hanging over his wife.]
EMILIA. Yes, throw yourself down and howl, because you've killed the sweetest innocent who ever lifted her eyes to heaven.
OTHELLO. Oh, she was filthy! I hardly recognized you, uncle. There lies your niece, whose breath, it's true, these hands have just now stopped. I know this deed looks horrible and grim.

GRATIANO. Poor Desdemona! I'm glad your father's dead. Your marriage was deadly to him, and grief alone cut the thread of his old life in two. If he were alive now, this sight would drive him to some desperate act — yes, he'd curse his guardian angel away from his side and fall into damnation.

OTHELLO. It's pitiful. But still, Iago knows that she's committed the shameful act with Cassio a thousand times. Cassio confessed it, and she rewarded his lovemaking with that keepsake and pledge of love that I first gave her. I saw it in his hand: it was a handkerchief, an old token my father gave my mother.
EMILIA. Oh, heaven! Oh, powers of heaven!
IAGO. Come on, be quiet.
EMILIA. It'll come out, it'll come out. Me, be quiet? No, I'll speak as freely as the north wind blows. Let heaven and men and devils, let them all, all, all cry shame on me — I'll still speak.
IAGO. Be sensible, and go home.
EMILIA. I will not.
[Iago offers to stab his wife.]
GRATIANO. Shame on you! Your sword against a woman?

EMILIA. Oh, you stupid Moor, that handkerchief you're talking about — I found it by chance and gave it to my husband; because again and again, with a serious intensity far greater than such a little thing really deserved, he begged me to steal it.
IAGO. You villainous whore!
EMILIA. She gave it to Cassio? No, oh no, I found it, and I gave it to my husband.
IAGO. You filth, you're lying!
EMILIA. By heaven, I'm not, I'm not, gentlemen. Oh, you murderous fool! What would a fool like you do with a wife as good as yours?
[OTHELLO Are there no thunderbolts in heaven except the ones it needs for thunder? You utter villain!]
[Iago stabs Emilia and then runs out.]
GRATIANO. The woman's falling. He's surely killed his wife.
EMILIA. Yes, yes. Oh, lay me beside my mistress.
GRATIANO. He's gone, but his wife's been killed.

MONTANO. He's a notorious villain. Take this weapon, which I've just taken from the Moor. Come, guard the door from the outside; don't let the Moor through — kill him instead. I'll go after that villain Iago, because he's a damned wretch.
[Exit Montano and Gratiano.]
OTHELLO. I'm not brave anymore, either — every puny little whippersnapper can take my sword. But why should honor outlive honesty? Let it all go.

EMILIA. What did your song foretell, lady? Listen, can you hear me? I'll be like the swan and die singing. _Willow, willow, willow._ Moor, she was chaste. She loved you, cruel Moor. May my soul go to heaven as surely as I speak the truth; and saying what I think, I die, I die.
[She dies.]
OTHELLO. I have another weapon in this room: it's a Spanish sword, tempered in an icy stream. Oh, here it is. — Uncle, I have to come out.
GRATIANO. If you try it, it'll cost you dearly. You have no weapon, and you'll have to put up with it.
OTHELLO. Then come in here and talk to me, or, unarmed as I am, I'll attack you.
[Enter Gratiano.]
GRATIANO. What's the matter?

OTHELLO. Look, I have a weapon. No better sword ever hung at a soldier's thigh.
