I've seen the day when, with this little arm and this good sword, I cut my way through more obstacles than twenty times what you put in my way. But, oh, what an empty boast! Who can control his fate? It's not like that now. Don't be afraid, even though you see me armed. Here's my journey's end, here's my finish line, my target, the very landmark that shows where my last voyage ends. Are you backing away in fear? It's a wasted fear. Just point a reed at Othello's chest and he'll retreat. Where would Othello go? Now, how do you look now? Oh, ill-fated girl, pale as your nightgown! When we meet on Judgment Day, this look of yours will hurl my soul out of heaven, and demons will snatch at it. Cold, cold, my girl! Just like your chastity. Oh, cursed, cursed wretch that I am! Whip me, you devils, away from the sight of this heavenly creature! Blow me around in the winds, roast me in burning sulfur, wash me in sheer-sided pits of liquid fire! Oh, Desdemona! Dead, Desdemona! Dead! Oh, oh!
[Enter Lodovico, Montano, Cassio carried in a chair, and Officers with Iago prisoner.]
LODOVICO. Where is this reckless and most unfortunate man?
OTHELLO. That's the man who used to be Othello. Here I am.
LODOVICO. Where is that snake? Bring the villain out.
OTHELLO. I look down at his feet for cloven hooves — but that's just a fairy tale. If you really are a devil, I can't kill you.
[Wounds Iago.]
LODOVICO. Wrestle his sword away from him.
IAGO. I'm bleeding, sir, but not killed.
OTHELLO. I'm not sorry about that either. I'd rather you lived, because the way I feel, it's happiness to die.
LODOVICO. Oh, you, Othello, who were once so good, brought down by the schemes of a damned wretch, what can anyone say to you?
OTHELLO. Why, anything: an honorable murderer, if you like, because I did nothing out of hate, but everything for honor.
LODOVICO. This wretch has partly confessed his villainy. Did you and he agree to kill Cassio?
OTHELLO. Yes.
CASSIO. Dear general, I never gave you any reason.
OTHELLO. I believe it, and I ask your forgiveness. Will you please ask that half-devil why he's trapped my soul and body like this?
IAGO. Don't ask me anything. What you know, you know. From now on I'll never say a word.
LODOVICO. What, not even to pray?
GRATIANO. Torture will open your lips.
OTHELLO. Well, keeping quiet is the best thing you can do.

LODOVICO. Sir, you need to understand what's happened, which I don't think you know yet. Here's a letter found in the pocket of the murdered Roderigo, and here's another. One of them says that the killing of Cassio was to be carried out by Roderigo.
OTHELLO. Oh, villain!
CASSIO. Utterly godless and monstrous!

LODOVICO. Now here's another letter, full of complaints, found in his pocket too; and it seems Roderigo meant to send this to that damned villain, except that Iago, most likely, in the meantime came by and gave him an answer that satisfied him.
OTHELLO. Oh, the evil wretch! — How did you get hold of that handkerchief, Cassio, the one that was my wife's?
CASSIO. I found it in my room. And he himself confessed just now that he dropped it there on purpose, and it worked just the way he wanted.
OTHELLO. Oh, fool! Fool! Fool!

CASSIO. On top of that, in Roderigo's letter he scolds Iago for making him pick a fight with me on watch duty, which is how it came about that I was dismissed. And just now he spoke — after lying there a long time seeming dead — saying Iago stabbed him, Iago put him up to it.

LODOVICO. You must leave this room and come with us. Your power and your command are taken from you, and Cassio governs Cyprus. As for this wretch, if there's any ingenious cruelty that can torture him a lot and keep him alive a long time, it'll be his. You'll stay a closely guarded prisoner until the details of your crime are reported to the Venetian government. Come, take him away.

OTHELLO. Wait a moment; a word or two before you go. I've done the state some service, and they know it. Enough about that. I ask you, in your letters, when you report these unhappy events, speak of me as I am. Don't make excuses for anything, or write anything down out of malice. Then you must speak of one who loved not wisely, but too well; of one who wasn't easily jealous, but once worked on, was distraught beyond all measure; of one whose hand, like the vile Judean, threw away a pearl worth more than his whole tribe; of one whose lowered eyes, though they're not used to melting into tears, drop tears as fast as the Arabian trees drip their healing gum. Write this down. And say as well that in Aleppo once, when a vicious Turk in a turban was beating a Venetian and insulting the Venetian state, I took the circumcised dog by the throat and struck him — like this.
[Stabs himself.]
LODOVICO. Oh, bloody ending!
GRATIANO. That ruins everything he said.
OTHELLO. I kissed you before I killed you. There's no other way than this: killing myself, to die upon a kiss.
[Falling upon Desdemona.]
CASSIO. I was afraid of this — though I thought he had no weapon — because he had a great heart.

LODOVICO. Oh, you Spartan dog, savage and silent, more deadly than pain, hunger, or the sea, look at the tragic load on this bed. This is your work. The sight poisons the eyes; cover it up. Gratiano, take charge of the house and take possession of the Moor's property, because it passes on to you as heir. To you, lord governor, falls the sentencing of this hellish villain: the time, the place, the torture — oh, make sure it's carried out! I'll go on board ship right away, and with a heavy heart report this heavy deed to the state.
[Exeunt.]
